## Introduction

Arrhythmia is a disorder of cardiac impulse generation, impulse conduction, or both, resulting in abnormal heart rhythm that can range from benign irregularity to life threatening electrical instability (Disease code: arrhythmia). In the analysis of the United Kingdom Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project data, circulating levels of 503 plasma proteins were found to be significantly associated with arrhythmia, based on 28,952 controls and 3,926 cases, after Bonferroni correction at P < 0.000000001. Understanding the biological basis of arrhythmia reflected by these 503 proteins is essential because rhythm disorders arise from the interaction of electrophysiological dysfunction, structural remodeling, inflammation, and systemic disease processes, and protein level associations provide a quantitative entry point for mapping these mechanisms.

To define the molecular landscape underlying these protein associations, we performed a comprehensive functional enrichment analysis on the 503 proteins using pathway resources spanning Gene Ontology Molecular Function, Gene Ontology Biological Process, Gene Ontology Cellular Component, Reactome, and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes. Across these resources, we identified 84 significantly enriched biological pathways (Table 1). The enrichment profile indicates that arrhythmia associated proteins are concentrated in several coherent biological themes. The strongest signals point to cytokine mediated and immune related mechanisms, including cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction with 65 associated proteins and a P value of 1.0480055801033972 × 10−34, viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor with 27 associated proteins and a P value of 4.277640489045937 × 10−16, tumor necrosis factors bind their physiological receptors with 14 associated proteins and a P value of 1.299783594479869 × 10−11, and neutrophil degranulation with 48 associated proteins and a P value of 5.793716961483522 × 10−10. These results support a major contribution of inflammatory signaling, innate immune activation, and cytokine driven tissue responses to arrhythmia biology.

A second major theme is extracellular matrix organization and fibrotic remodeling, highlighted by enrichment of collagen metabolic process with 14 associated proteins and a P value of 3.1440856737905816 × 10−7, glycosaminoglycan binding with 30 associated proteins and a P value of 5.378474612832188 × 10−15, lung fibrosis with 15 associated proteins and a P value of 8.265656098006917 × 10−7, and endopeptidase activity with 44 associated proteins and a P value of 2.7954040457582796 × 10−11. These pathways suggest that matrix turnover, proteolytic remodeling, and fibrosis related programs may contribute to the structural substrate that destabilizes cardiac conduction. Additional enrichment in lipid localization with 26 associated proteins and a P value of 3.415223569846427 × 10−5, late endosome with 16 associated proteins and a P value of 0.007816926593059137, and ruffle membrane with 6 associated proteins and a P value of 0.041994677647457415 further indicates that membrane organization, intracellular trafficking, and lipid handling may also shape arrhythmia susceptibility through effects on receptor turnover, signaling, and ion channel localization.

Taken together, these 84 enriched pathways show that arrhythmia is represented not by a single isolated mechanism but by a broad molecular network involving inflammatory signaling, immune regulation, extracellular matrix remodeling, fibrosis, proteolysis, and membrane trafficking. In the following sections, we examine the most significant pathways and their associated protein interactions in greater detail to clarify how these processes may contribute to the molecular framework of arrhythmia.

## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways associated with arrhythmia on the basis of statistical significance, biological coherence, and disease relevance. The overall enrichment pattern is dominated by inflammatory and cytokine-mediated mechanisms. The most statistically significant signal is cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04060, p = 1.0480055801033972 × 10−34, 65 associated proteins), followed by viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04061, p = 4.277640489045937 × 10−16, 27 associated proteins), tumor necrosis factors bind their physiological receptors (Reactome:R-HSA-5669034, p = 1.299783594479869 × 10−11, 14 associated proteins), and neutrophil degranulation (Reactome:R-HSA-6798695, p = 5.793716961483522 × 10−10, 48 associated proteins). Taken together, these very low p-values and relatively large associated protein counts suggest a robust enrichment signal centered on immune activation. This pattern is consistent with literature indicating that inflammatory cytokines, innate immune activation, and infection-related signaling may alter ion channel function, gap junction coupling, calcium handling, and atrial or ventricular structural remodeling, thereby increasing susceptibility to arrhythmia.  

This inflammatory profile also connects naturally to a second major theme in the enrichment results, namely extracellular matrix turnover and tissue remodeling. Strong enrichment of collagen metabolic process (Gene Ontology:0032963, p = 3.1440856737905816 × 10−7, 14 associated proteins), glycosaminoglycan binding (Gene Ontology:0005539, p = 5.378474612832188 × 10−15, 30 associated proteins), and lung fibrosis (WikiPathways:WP3624, p = 8.265656098006917 × 10−7, 15 associated proteins) suggests that fibrotic remodeling may represent an important shared mechanism. This interpretation is supported by cardiac literature showing that excess collagen deposition and extracellular matrix reorganization can disrupt electrical conduction, promote conduction heterogeneity, and facilitate re-entry, which are central mechanisms in many forms of arrhythmia. The enrichment of endopeptidase activity (Gene Ontology:0004175, p = 2.7954040457582796 × 10−11, 44 associated proteins) further supports the possibility of active proteolytic remodeling of the extracellular environment, which may contribute to myocardial fibrosis and inflammatory tissue injury.  

Beyond inflammation and matrix remodeling, the enrichment profile may also point to changes in membrane organization and intracellular transport. Additional pathways, including lipid localization (Gene Ontology:0010876, p = 3.415223569846427 × 10−5, 26 associated proteins), late endosome (Gene Ontology:0005770, p = 0.007816926593059137, 16 associated proteins), and ruffle membrane (Gene Ontology:0032587, p = 0.041994677647457415, 6 associated proteins), suggest altered membrane trafficking, lipid handling, and receptor turnover. These processes are relevant because membrane composition and intracellular trafficking can influence ion channel localization, receptor signaling, and cardiomyocyte stress responses, all of which have been implicated in arrhythmia biology. Although some enriched annotations, such as colon goblet cells (Human Protein Atlas:0130891, p = 3.96653314155423 × 10−6, 36 associated proteins; Human Protein Atlas:0130893, p = 6.70451993364627 × 10−5, 21 associated proteins), pleural mesothelioma (WikiPathways:WP5087, p = 5.1660111075016064 × 10−5, 38 associated proteins), and arthralgia (Human Phenotype Ontology:0002829, p = 0.020265199832114434, 20 associated proteins), are less directly related to cardiac biology, they may reflect shared inflammatory, extracellular matrix, and secretory programs rather than tissue-specific causation. Overall, the pathway profile supports a model in which arrhythmia is linked to a convergence of cytokine-driven inflammation, immune cell activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, fibrosis, and altered membrane trafficking, with the very low p-values providing strong statistical support for these mechanisms.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

With this overall enrichment structure in view, the following sections provide a more detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### Arthralgia (HP:0002829) 

Arthralgia refers to joint pain and is a clinical symptom rather than a discrete molecular signaling pathway. In biomedical interpretation, it usually reflects one of several underlying biological contexts, including systemic inflammation, autoimmune activation, infection-associated immune responses, metabolic or electrolyte disturbance, or treatment-related toxicity. Because joint pain commonly accompanies disorders with broad inflammatory or immune involvement, it can function as a clinical marker of multisystem disease rather than an isolated musculoskeletal complaint. The publications provided show that arthralgia appears in several settings relevant to heart rhythm disorders: as an adverse effect of anticancer therapy with Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibition, as a symptom in autoimmune diseases such as primary Sjogren syndrome and sarcoidosis, as part of infectious syndromes such as dengue, Lyme disease, and Zika virus infection, and in association with metabolic derangements such as severe magnesium deficiency. Thus, the biological significance of arthralgia in the present context is that it may identify disease states or treatment exposures that also affect cardiac conduction tissue, atrial and ventricular myocardium, autonomic balance, blood pressure regulation, calcium handling, or inflammatory injury, all of which can promote arrhythmia.  

Building on this clinical framing, the relationship between arthralgia and arrhythmia appears to be predominantly indirect, yet still clinically meaningful, because arthralgia often co-occurs with systemic conditions that may create an arrhythmogenic substrate. In autoimmune disease, transient or inflammatory arthralgia may accompany disorders with direct cardiac involvement; for example, primary Sjogren syndrome presenting with dry mouth and arthralgia was associated with complex arrhythmias, atrioventricular node dysfunction, and intraventricular conduction impairment, with improvement after glucocorticoid treatment, supporting an inflammatory mechanism linking the systemic syndrome to electrical instability of the heart (PubMed:26171561). A similar pattern is seen in sarcoidosis, in which arthralgia can accompany granulomatous disease that may involve the myocardium and lead to ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, conduction disease, arrhythmias, and heart failure (PubMed:36174882, PubMed:27454307). Infectious illnesses also illustrate this connection: dengue commonly presents with fever, myalgia, and arthralgia, yet can be complicated by atrial fibrillation and other rhythm disturbances, possibly through myocarditis, inflammatory cytokine activation, and altered intracellular calcium handling (PubMed:26500943, PubMed:38205141). Lyme disease and Zika virus infection likewise include arthralgia among systemic manifestations while also being linked to atrial fibrillation, atrioventricular block, myocarditis, and broader arrhythmic complications (PubMed:39391111, PubMed:33220438). Arthralgia may additionally signal treatment exposure relevant to arrhythmia risk: in trials of Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors, arthralgia was a common adverse event, whereas atrial fibrillation and hypertension were notable cardiac toxicities, particularly with ibrutinib-containing therapy, indicating that joint pain and arrhythmia can emerge within the same drug-toxicity profile even if one does not directly cause the other (PubMed:29856685, PubMed:36400069). Finally, the coexistence of arthralgia and atrial fibrillation in severe magnesium deficiency emphasizes that shared systemic disturbances can produce both musculoskeletal symptoms and electrical instability (PubMed:31776649). Collectively, these studies indicate that arthralgia should be interpreted in arrhythmia research and clinical practice as a sentinel symptom of inflammatory, infectious, autoimmune, metabolic, or pharmacological states that may secondarily disrupt cardiac electrophysiology.[PubMed:36400069](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36400069) [PubMed:29856685](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29856685) [PubMed:26171561](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26171561) [PubMed:36174882](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36174882) [PubMed:26500943](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26500943) [PubMed:31776649](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31776649) [PubMed:39391111](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39391111) [PubMed:33220438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33220438) [PubMed:27454307](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27454307) [PubMed:38205141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38205141) 

With this clinical context in mind, the enrichment analysis may be viewed as a complementary layer that connects the symptom-level signal of arthralgia to biological processes potentially relevant to cardiac electrical instability. There were 20 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the biological context represented by arthralgia, which in this setting should be interpreted not as a single molecular pathway but as a clinically informative enrichment signal linking joint pain with systemic inflammation, autoimmune activation, infection-related immune responses, metabolic disturbance, treatment toxicity, and cardiac electrophysiological vulnerability. This enrichment pattern is biologically relevant to arrhythmia because the underlying conditions associated with arthralgia can converge on several arrhythmia-promoting mechanisms, including inflammatory injury to atrial and ventricular myocardium, altered autonomic regulation, disturbed calcium and magnesium homeostasis, blood pressure instability, and conduction system involvement. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 20 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration.

To move from the network-level view to gene-level interpretation, the following section introduces several proteins that may be of particular interest in relation to arrhythmia, while keeping the discussion cautious and grounded in the functions provided. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Among the listed proteins, ELN is one of the most compelling candidates for a meaningful connection with arrhythmia because abnormalities in elastin biology can directly affect vascular mechanics, ventricular afterload, and myocardial structural remodeling. ELN is essential for the mechanical integrity and elasticity of the aorta and other large vessels, and its role in smooth muscle cell maturation and extracellular matrix organization suggests that its dysfunction could promote arterial stiffness, altered hemodynamics, and secondary cardiac remodeling. Such remodeling is a well-established substrate for atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. In addition, ELN participates in collagen fibril assembly and elastin cross-linking via LOX-related pathways, linking it to broader fibrotic and matrix-remodeling processes that can disrupt electrical conduction indirectly through myocardial fibrosis. Its reported involvement in angiotensin-related vascular smooth muscle regulation is also notable, because renin-angiotensin signaling is strongly implicated in atrial fibrosis and arrhythmogenesis. Therefore, although ELN is not a classical ion-channel gene, it stands out as a plausible contributor to arrhythmia susceptibility through vascular dysfunction, extracellular matrix remodeling, and electromechanical coupling abnormalities.[PubMed:16478991](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16478991) [PubMed:19855011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19855011) [PubMed:20019329](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019329) [PubMed:26486174](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26486174) [PubMed:26711913](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26711913) [PubMed:28508064](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28508064) [PubMed:26178373](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26178373) [PubMed:26220971](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26220971) [PubMed:26690653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26690653) [PubMed:17324935](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17324935) [PubMed:23636094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23636094) 

Continuing from extracellular elastic structure to broader matrix organization, COL5A1 is relevant to arrhythmia primarily through its role in extracellular matrix architecture. Although type V collagen is a relatively minor fibrillar collagen, it is important in connective tissue organization and likely influences collagen fibrillogenesis and tissue mechanical properties. In the heart, perturbation of collagen composition can alter myocardial stiffness, chamber compliance, and conduction properties by promoting interstitial fibrosis or abnormal matrix organization. These changes are central to the development of arrhythmogenic substrates, particularly in atrial fibrillation and scar-related ventricular arrhythmias. The ability of COL5A1 to interact with matrix-associated molecules such as thrombospondin and glycosaminoglycans further supports a role in broader matrix signaling networks. Thus, COL5A1 stands out as a structurally relevant gene whose dysregulation could contribute indirectly to arrhythmia by modifying myocardial extracellular matrix composition and favoring conduction heterogeneity.  

Shifting from extracellular structure to nuclear organization, LMNB2 is noteworthy because defects in nuclear envelope biology are increasingly recognized in cardiomyopathy syndromes that carry substantial arrhythmic risk. The nuclear lamina is critical for maintaining nuclear structural integrity and regulating chromatin organization, and disruption of these processes can alter gene expression programs essential for cardiomyocyte survival, mechanical resilience, and electrical stability. While LMNA is the prototypical lamin gene associated with conduction disease and malignant ventricular arrhythmias, the functions described for LMNB2 place it in a related biological framework. Disturbance of nuclear architecture may predispose to myocardial dysfunction, cellular stress responses, and maladaptive remodeling, all of which can create an arrhythmogenic substrate. Therefore, LMNB2 should be considered a potentially relevant structural-regulatory factor, especially in the context of inherited cardiomyopathy or conduction system disease.[PubMed:28241138](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28241138)  

From structural remodeling, the discussion next extends to cardiometabolic mechanisms. PCSK9 is highly relevant to arrhythmia from a cardiometabolic perspective. Its central role in low-density lipoprotein receptor degradation and cholesterol homeostasis links it strongly to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, ischemic myocardial injury, and subsequent scar formation, all of which are major substrates for ventricular arrhythmias. Beyond this indirect but clinically important connection, PCSK9 also influences receptor trafficking and proteostatic pathways, suggesting broader effects on cellular stress responses. The reported reduction of epithelial sodium channel surface expression is not a canonical cardiac arrhythmia mechanism, but it underscores that PCSK9 can modulate membrane protein abundance. In practice, the strongest arrhythmia-related relevance of PCSK9 is likely through promotion of coronary artery disease and ischemic remodeling, which increase the risk of atrial and ventricular rhythm disorders. Thus, PCSK9 stands out not as a direct electrophysiological determinant, but as an important upstream driver of structural heart disease that can culminate in arrhythmogenesis.[PubMed:18039658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039658) [PubMed:17461796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17461796) [PubMed:18197702](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18197702) [PubMed:18799458](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18799458) [PubMed:22074827](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22074827) [PubMed:18660751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18660751) 

A related but more inflammation-centered mechanism is suggested by PRTN3. PRTN3 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because it links inflammation, vascular injury, and extracellular matrix degradation. Its proteolytic activity against elastin, laminin, fibronectin, and multiple collagens indicates a capacity to remodel tissue architecture extensively. In the cardiovascular system, excessive matrix degradation and inflammatory activation can contribute to endothelial dysfunction, myocardial injury, and fibrotic repair, all of which favor conduction abnormalities. The ability of PRTN3 to trigger inflammatory processes in neutrophils and participate in transendothelial migration further strengthens a plausible role in inflammatory arrhythmogenesis, particularly in settings such as myocarditis, vascular inflammation, or post-ischemic remodeling. Since inflammation is a recognized contributor to atrial fibrillation and other rhythm disorders, PRTN3 stands out as a biologically credible mediator of arrhythmia risk through immune-proteolytic pathways rather than direct ion-channel effects.[PubMed:2033050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2033050) [PubMed:28240246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28240246) [PubMed:3198760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3198760) [PubMed:23202369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23202369) [PubMed:22266279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22266279) [PubMed:36302784](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36302784) 

Because systemic mineral regulation is another recurring theme in arrhythmia biology, PTH1R may also warrant attention. PTH1R is particularly relevant to arrhythmia because calcium homeostasis is fundamental to cardiac excitability, action potential dynamics, and excitation-contraction coupling. Through its role in systemic calcium regulation, altered PTH1R signaling could contribute to hypercalcemia or broader calcium imbalance, both of which are known to affect cardiac conduction and repolarization. Clinically, disturbances in calcium metabolism can precipitate atrial and ventricular arrhythmias by modifying threshold potentials, triggered activity, and refractoriness. Although the function provided is centered on bone and renal calcium handling rather than direct cardiac signaling, the mechanistic link to arrhythmia is strong because systemic calcium perturbation is itself arrhythmogenic. Therefore, PTH1R deserves attention as an indirect but physiologically important determinant of rhythm stability.  

Extending from calcium balance to immune-remodeling interactions, SPP1 is a notable candidate because it connects immune activation with tissue remodeling, a combination highly relevant to arrhythmia. The described cytokine profile indicates a pro-inflammatory immune phenotype, favoring type I immune responses. In the heart, chronic inflammation promotes fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix deposition, and electrical heterogeneity, particularly in atrial tissue. SPP1, also widely known as osteopontin, has been implicated in fibrotic and inflammatory remodeling in multiple cardiovascular contexts, making its inclusion particularly interesting. Even based solely on the listed function, its capacity to skew cytokine production toward a pro-inflammatory state supports a plausible role in atrial fibrillation, post-injury remodeling, and myocarditis-associated arrhythmias. Thus, SPP1 stands out as a likely mediator of inflammation-driven arrhythmogenic remodeling.  

A mechanistically related line of reasoning applies to TNFRSF11B. TNFRSF11B is of interest for arrhythmia because the function described prominently features intracellular calcium oscillations and reactive oxygen species generation, two processes that are central to cardiac arrhythmogenesis. Although the annotated context is osteoclast differentiation, the signaling logic is highly relevant: prolonged calcium oscillations and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species are known to promote triggered activity, cellular stress, and remodeling in cardiomyocytes. In addition, its immunoregulatory functions suggest a potential role in inflammatory disease states that can secondarily affect the myocardium. Therefore, TNFRSF11B may not be a direct arrhythmia gene in the classical sense, but it stands out mechanistically because it operates in pathways—calcium signaling, reactive oxygen species production, and immune regulation—that are deeply implicated in rhythm disorders.[PubMed:22664871](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22664871)  

In a similar tentative framework, TNFRSF13B may be relevant through protein handling and calcium-linked signaling. TNFRSF13B is potentially relevant to arrhythmia through two main mechanisms. First, its role in tail-anchored protein delivery to the endoplasmic reticulum suggests it contributes to membrane protein biogenesis and trafficking, processes that are highly important for ion channels and other proteins governing cardiac excitability. Disruption of protein targeting or membrane insertion can alter cellular electrophysiology indirectly. Second, its involvement in intracellular calcium elevation, although described in T cells, points to broader biology connected to calcium signaling, a core determinant of arrhythmia. Its role in B-cell survival also raises the possibility of immune-mediated effects on cardiac tissue in inflammatory settings. Overall, TNFRSF13B is not the strongest arrhythmia candidate on the list, but it is mechanistically interesting because it intersects protein trafficking, calcium signaling, and immunity.[PubMed:23041287](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23041287) [PubMed:24392163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24392163) [PubMed:27226539](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27226539) [PubMed:32187542](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32187542) [PubMed:7522304](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7522304)  

The immune-remodeling theme becomes even more apparent when considering TREM2. TREM2 stands out because it is deeply involved in innate immune activation and phagocytic responses, processes increasingly recognized as important in arrhythmia-associated cardiac remodeling. The broad immune signaling functions described here suggest that TREM2 can shape inflammatory tone, cytokine production, cell survival, and tissue remodeling. In the setting of cardiac injury, myocarditis, or chronic heart failure, dysregulated myeloid activation and macrophage behavior can promote fibrosis, alter gap-junction organization, and destabilize electrical conduction. TREM2-related pathways may therefore influence arrhythmia susceptibility indirectly through inflammatory remodeling rather than direct electrophysiological effects. Its role in multinucleated giant cell formation and osteoclast biology also reinforces its involvement in fusion and cytoskeletal programs that may mirror broader tissue-remodeling functions. Overall, TREM2 is a strong immunobiological candidate for contributing to arrhythmogenic substrates in inflammatory or remodeling-prone cardiovascular disease.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392)  

Finally, complementing the structural, inflammatory, and metabolic candidates above, ADA2 introduces a neurohumoral dimension that may also be relevant to rhythm regulation. ADA2 is directly relevant to arrhythmia because adrenergic signaling is a major regulator of heart rate, conduction, and triggered electrical activity. Alpha-2 adrenergic receptors modulate cyclic adenosine monophosphate generation through G-protein-mediated inhibition of adenylate cyclase, thereby influencing autonomic balance. Since sympathetic and parasympathetic tone strongly affect arrhythmia initiation and maintenance, especially in atrial fibrillation and stress-triggered ventricular arrhythmias, altered ADA2-related signaling could plausibly modify arrhythmia susceptibility. Although this receptor is not as classically implicated as beta-adrenergic pathways in cardiac electrophysiology, catecholamine signaling broadly is central to arrhythmic risk. Therefore, ADA2 is a noteworthy candidate because it connects neurohumoral regulation to electrophysiological instability.

### Colon; goblet cells[≥Low] (HPA:0130891) 

The pathway described as colon goblet cells at low abundance refers to a biological state in which mucus-secreting epithelial cells of the colon are reduced in number or function. Colon goblet cells are central to intestinal barrier integrity because they synthesize and secrete mucin two and related protective products that form the mucus layer separating luminal microorganisms from the epithelium. The cited literature indicates that loss of goblet cells disrupts the inner mucus layer, facilitates bacterial translocation, and amplifies local and systemic inflammatory signaling. In experimental graft-versus-host disease, depletion of colon goblet cells increased bacterial penetration into the mucosa and was associated with elevated circulating interferon gamma and interleukin six, whereas preservation of goblet cells improved barrier function and reduced inflammatory burden (PubMed:32611682). Mechanistically, goblet cell differentiation and maturation are regulated by pathways such as Notch signaling, bone morphogenetic protein signaling, and factors including dedicator of cytokinesis four, growth factor independent one, and SAM pointed domain containing ETS transcription factor; disruption of these programs lowers goblet cell abundance and mucin production (PubMed:38684650, PubMed:33559155, PubMed:34121974). Additional studies further show that reduced goblet cells accompany impaired epithelial trafficking, lower trefoil factor three positivity, weakened tight junction expression, and heightened susceptibility to inflammatory injury, all of which are consistent with a compromised intestinal barrier state (PubMed:35819177, PubMed:40362775). Taken together, this pathway may be understood as a marker of defective colonic mucosal defense, enhanced host-microbiota contact, and increased potential for systemic immune and metabolic consequences.  

This broader barrier-defect framework also provides a useful transition to the possible cardiovascular relevance of the pathway. The available publications do not identify a direct, heart-specific electrophysiological role for colon goblet cells in arrhythmia; however, they support an indirect but biologically plausible connection through the intestine-heart axis. When colon goblet cells are reduced, the mucus barrier becomes defective, allowing greater microbial translocation and exaggerated inflammatory signaling, including increases in circulating interleukin six and interferon gamma, as shown in the graft-versus-host disease study by Ara and colleagues (PubMed:32611682). This observation is relevant to arrhythmia because systemic inflammation is a well-established promoter of atrial and ventricular electrical instability through effects on ion channel regulation, autonomic tone, calcium handling, and structural remodeling. The goblet cell pathway also intersects with epithelial differentiation programs such as Notch signaling and bone morphogenetic protein signaling; perturbation of these pathways changes secretory cell balance and mucus production in the human colon (PubMed:38684650, PubMed:34121974), suggesting that sustained epithelial dysregulation could perpetuate chronic intestinal inflammatory signaling. Studies of dedicator of cytokinesis four deficiency, Rab11 family interacting protein one deficiency, nutritional protein restriction, and glutamate rescue further indicate that goblet cell loss is consistently linked to reduced mucin production, impaired barrier proteins, and greater inflammatory susceptibility (PubMed:33559155, PubMed:35819177, PubMed:37197734, PubMed:40362775). In aggregate, low colon goblet cell abundance may therefore be interpreted as a potential upstream contributor to arrhythmia risk, not by direct cardiac expression, but by fostering microbial translocation, cytokinemia, and metabolic disturbance that can create a pro-arrhythmic systemic milieu.[PubMed:32611682](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32611682) [PubMed:38684650](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38684650) [PubMed:33559155](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33559155) [PubMed:34121974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34121974) [PubMed:35819177](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35819177) [PubMed:37197734](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37197734) [PubMed:40362775](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40362775) 

Building on this biological interpretation, the enrichment results suggest that this pathway may capture a systemically relevant inflammatory and barrier-related signature within the arrhythmia-associated protein set. There were 36 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway described as colon goblet cells at low abundance, a functional state defined by reduced mucus-secreting epithelial cell number or activity, impaired mucin two production, weakened intestinal barrier integrity, greater microbial contact with the colonic epithelium, and increased inflammatory spillover into the systemic circulation. This enrichment is biologically notable because the pathway captures a barrier-defect phenotype in which goblet cell depletion is linked to higher bacterial penetration, elevated interferon gamma and interleukin six, disrupted epithelial differentiation programs involving Notch signaling and bone morphogenetic protein signaling, and reduced expression of protective epithelial factors, collectively indicating that the 36-protein set converges on mechanisms with plausible inflammatory and systemic consequences relevant to arrhythmia pathobiology (PubMed:32611682, PubMed:38684650, PubMed:33559155, PubMed:34121974, PubMed:35819177, PubMed:40362775). With this network-level context in place, the individual proteins can be considered in turn according to their possible relevance to arrhythmia biology. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
YAP1 stands out as one of the most arrhythmia-relevant proteins in this list because Hippo-YAP signaling is a central regulator of cardiomyocyte growth, survival, mechanotransduction, and electrical remodeling. Although the provided annotation is concise, its ability to activate ERBB4 signaling is potentially important in the heart, where ERBB family pathways influence myocardial development, stress responses, and cell-cell communication. In arrhythmia, disturbed mechanosignaling and maladaptive remodeling frequently alter conduction velocity, repolarization stability, and susceptibility to re-entry. YAP1 is therefore relevant not because it is explicitly annotated here as an ion-channel regulator, but because it may participate upstream of structural and transcriptional programs that shape arrhythmogenic substrate, including fibrosis, hypertrophy, and altered excitation-contraction coupling. This makes YAP1 a plausible modifier of arrhythmia risk, particularly in disease states characterized by myocardial remodeling.  

A related theme of tissue architecture and intercellular organization is also reflected in the next candidate. CDH1 encodes E-cadherin, a canonical cell-cell adhesion molecule, and despite the annotation emphasizing microbial entry, its broader biological role makes it highly relevant to arrhythmia. Cardiac rhythm stability depends critically on intact intercellular adhesion at the intercalated disc, where mechanical junctions are tightly coupled to electrical coupling machinery. Even though CDH1 is not the dominant cadherin in adult myocardium compared with desmosomal and adherens junction components such as N-cadherin, cadherin-mediated adhesion is conceptually central to conduction integrity. Disruption of epithelial or myocardial adhesive architecture can promote tissue disorganization, altered gap-junction localization, slowed conduction, and re-entrant arrhythmias. Thus, CDH1 is notable as a structural adhesion-related protein whose dysfunction may intersect with arrhythmogenic mechanisms through effects on tissue cohesion and cell signaling.  

This structural perspective extends further to membrane-associated remodeling factors. BSG is of potential interest for arrhythmia primarily through its broader identity as basigin/CD147, a multifunctional membrane glycoprotein involved in cell adhesion, extracellular signaling, and tissue remodeling. The annotation provided is neurobiological, but these properties still suggest relevance to cardiac electrophysiology because arrhythmia often emerges from pathological remodeling rather than ion-channel dysfunction alone. Adhesion molecules and glycan-recognition pathways can influence cellular interactions, inflammatory signaling, and extracellular matrix turnover, all of which contribute to conduction heterogeneity. In particular, proteins with broad roles in membrane organization and tissue maintenance may affect the arrhythmogenic substrate in structurally diseased hearts. Therefore, BSG is noteworthy as a candidate indirect modulator of arrhythmia susceptibility through remodeling-related mechanisms.[PubMed:12089450](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [PubMed:27922006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [PubMed:7533044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [PubMed:10625334](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [PubMed:7516497](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [PubMed:9262180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [PubMed:9469574](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [PubMed:9482781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [PubMed:9482783](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [PubMed:26335717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [PubMed:15953602](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [PubMed:19158290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [PubMed:17640868](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868) 

From membrane organization, the discussion naturally shifts to cellular energetics, another major determinant of electrical stability. CHCHD10 is a particularly compelling candidate in the context of arrhythmia because mitochondrial integrity is essential for cardiac excitability and rhythm stability. The heart is highly dependent on oxidative metabolism, and disruption of mitochondrial cristae architecture can impair adenosine triphosphate production, increase reactive oxygen species generation, and alter calcium handling. These processes are directly linked to arrhythmogenic mechanisms, including triggered activity, impaired repolarization reserve, and conduction abnormalities in metabolically stressed myocardium. Although the annotation is brief, proteins that preserve mitochondrial ultrastructure are highly relevant to arrhythmia biology, especially in cardiomyopathies where energetic failure and electrical instability frequently coexist. CHCHD10 therefore stands out as a plausible contributor to arrhythmia through mitochondrial dysfunction-driven electrophysiological remodeling.  

At the tissue level, vascular and extracellular matrix regulation may add another layer of relevance. COL18A1 is relevant to arrhythmia because vascular remodeling, myocardial perfusion, and extracellular matrix organization are important determinants of the arrhythmogenic substrate. Its anti-angiogenic activity, particularly through interference with VEGFA-KDR/VEGFR2 signaling, suggests a role in regulating microvascular responses and tissue repair. In the diseased heart, impaired angiogenesis can exacerbate ischemia, fibrosis, and structural heterogeneity, all of which favor conduction slowing and re-entry. In addition, integrin-dependent effects on endothelial migration imply broader influence on matrix-cell interactions that may indirectly shape myocardial remodeling. Thus, while COL18A1 is not a classical electrophysiology gene, it is mechanistically relevant to arrhythmia through pathways linking vascular dysfunction, fibrosis, and structural remodeling.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

This remodeling-centered interpretation also connects well with inflammatory and infectious triggers of electrical instability. CXADR is one of the strongest arrhythmia-relevant proteins in this list because it links directly to viral infection, and Coxsackievirus infection is a well-established cause of myocarditis and subsequent arrhythmias. Viral myocarditis can produce atrial and ventricular arrhythmias through inflammatory injury, myocyte necrosis, edema, fibrosis, and conduction system involvement. Beyond its role as a viral receptor, CXADR is also known more broadly as a cell adhesion molecule at intercellular junctions, which is conceptually important for electrical propagation. Consequently, this protein may connect infectious triggers with structural and electrical remodeling of the myocardium. Its presence is therefore highly notable in any arrhythmia-oriented interpretation, especially in settings involving inflammatory cardiomyopathy or post-viral electrical instability.  

A broader systemic stress dimension is suggested by the next pathway-related annotation. The annotation provided corresponds to the GDF15 receptor pathway and is relevant to arrhythmia mainly as a marker and mediator of systemic stress signaling. GDF15 is strongly induced in cardiovascular disease, metabolic stress, inflammation, and tissue injury, all of which can influence arrhythmia risk. Activation of RET-MAPK-AKT signaling in stress-responsive circuits suggests broader integration of metabolic and neurohumoral responses. In clinical cardiology, elevated GDF15 is frequently associated with adverse outcomes, including atrial fibrillation burden, heart failure severity, and mortality, likely reflecting the extent of underlying myocardial stress and remodeling rather than a direct electrophysiological effect. Thus, this pathway is important as a biologically plausible contributor to arrhythmia susceptibility through stress adaptation, autonomic influences, and association with structural heart disease.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) 

Consistent with this stress and inflammation framework, iron metabolism and innate immune signaling may represent another plausible route to arrhythmogenic remodeling. LCN2 is highly relevant to arrhythmia because iron handling, inflammation, apoptosis, and cardiorenal interactions are all important determinants of electrical instability. The annotated functions indicate that LCN2 can alter intracellular iron availability and modulate apoptosis, both of which may influence oxidative stress and cellular survival in the myocardium. Excess redox-active iron promotes reactive oxygen species generation, which can disturb ion-channel function, calcium cycling, and gap-junction integrity. Moreover, its role in innate immunity suggests participation in inflammatory states that predispose to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. LCN2 is therefore notable as a potential mediator linking metabolic stress, inflammation, and tissue injury to arrhythmogenic remodeling, particularly in heart failure and systemic inflammatory disease.[PubMed:12453413](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12453413) [PubMed:15531878](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15531878) [PubMed:16446425](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16446425) 

Among inflammatory remodeling mediators, LGALS3 may deserve particular attention. LGALS3 is among the most important proteins in this list for arrhythmia because galectin-3 is a widely recognized mediator and biomarker of fibrosis and inflammation, two core mechanisms underlying atrial and ventricular arrhythmogenesis. The functions listed here support that interpretation: LGALS3 participates in inflammatory cell recruitment, endothelial migration, and damage-responsive autophagy, all of which can contribute to adverse cardiac remodeling. In arrhythmia, especially atrial fibrillation, inflammatory activation and extracellular matrix expansion create conduction heterogeneity and re-entry circuits. Galectin-3 has been repeatedly linked to fibrotic remodeling, heart failure progression, and arrhythmia recurrence after ablation. Therefore, even though the annotation does not explicitly mention fibrosis, the described immunoinflammatory and tissue-remodeling functions make LGALS3 a standout candidate with strong mechanistic relevance to arrhythmia.  

Another protein that may fit within this immune-remodeling axis is LGMN. LGMN is potentially relevant to arrhythmia through inflammatory and remodeling pathways. Its role in antigen presentation positions it within adaptive and innate immune responses, which are increasingly recognized as important in myocarditis, inflammatory cardiomyopathy, and atrial fibrillation. In addition, its involvement in EGFR degradation and cell proliferation suggests a role in tissue remodeling and cellular turnover. Because arrhythmias often arise in the setting of structural remodeling driven by inflammatory and growth-factor pathways, LGMN may contribute indirectly by shaping immune activation and receptor-signaling dynamics. This makes it a plausible secondary candidate in arrhythmia biology, especially in disease contexts characterized by immune-mediated myocardial injury or remodeling.[PubMed:23776206](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23776206) [PubMed:9872320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9872320) 

The analysis also points toward proteins involved in membrane domain organization, which may be relevant even when the primary annotation is not cardiac. NFASC is noteworthy because ankyrin-associated membrane scaffolding proteins are central to the organization of excitable membrane domains. Although the annotation is neural, the mechanistic theme is highly relevant to arrhythmia: proper localization of ion channels and adhesion complexes is essential for cardiac impulse initiation and propagation. Proteins that bind ankyrin often influence membrane excitability by stabilizing channel-rich domains, and disruption of such scaffolds can lead to conduction slowing or abnormal automaticity. NFASC therefore merits attention as an indirect arrhythmia-related candidate, particularly because shared principles of excitable-cell domain organization may extend from neurons to cardiomyocytes and the specialized conduction system.  

Returning to the broader intestine-immune interface highlighted by the pathway itself, mucosal defense proteins may also have indirect significance. PIGR is not a classical arrhythmia gene, but it may still be relevant through mucosal immunity and systemic inflammatory burden. Secretory IgA and IgM transport are critical for barrier defense, and disturbances in mucosal-immune homeostasis can contribute to chronic inflammation. Since inflammation is a major driver of atrial remodeling and arrhythmia susceptibility, proteins involved in immunoglobulin transport may have indirect importance. This is especially plausible in conditions where gut or airway inflammation contributes to systemic cytokine activation, autonomic imbalance, or pro-fibrotic signaling. Accordingly, PIGR should be viewed as a lower-priority but biologically plausible indirect modifier of arrhythmia risk.  

Finally, the set includes a candidate that may connect cellular stress responses with electrophysiological vulnerability. RNASE1, as annotated here through its inhibitor function and role in redox homeostasis, may be relevant to arrhythmia because oxidative stress is a major determinant of electrical instability. Redox imbalance can alter sodium, calcium, and potassium channel function, impair calcium handling, and promote both triggered activity and substrate remodeling. The described stress-responsive relocalization also suggests participation in adaptive cellular programs during injury. Although the connection is indirect, proteins involved in intracellular redox buffering and stress signaling may influence cardiomyocyte survival and electrophysiological stability under ischemic, inflammatory, or heart failure conditions. Thus, this entry is of moderate interest as a potential modifier of stress-related arrhythmogenesis.[PubMed:12578357](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12578357) [PubMed:14515218](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14515218) [PubMed:3219362](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3219362) [PubMed:3243277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3243277) [PubMed:3470787](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3470787) [PubMed:9050852](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9050852) [PubMed:17292889](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17292889) [PubMed:23843625](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23843625) [PubMed:32510170](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32510170)

### Colon; goblet cells[High] (HPA:0130893) 

This pathway refers to highly expressed goblet cell programs in the colon, particularly mature secretory epithelial cells that synthesize and release mucins to build the mucus barrier over the colonic surface. The cited literature indicates that colonic goblet cells are not a uniform population, but instead comprise functionally distinct subtypes distributed along the crypt to surface axis. A particularly important subtype is the intercrypt goblet cell population, which produces mucus that fills spaces between crypt-derived mucus plumes and contributes critically to a net-like barrier that prevents bacterial contact with the epithelium while still permitting selective diffusion of small molecules. Loss or dysfunction of these specialized goblet cells disrupts barrier integrity and increases susceptibility to colitis, suggesting that this pathway is central to epithelial protection, host and microbiota segregation, and mucosal immune homeostasis. Additional studies further indicate that goblet cell biology is closely linked to inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses, endoplasmic reticulum stress, hypoxia responses, and wound repair capacity. High mucin biosynthesis can impair restitution through endoplasmic reticulum stress and altered growth factor production, whereas hypoxia can reduce canonical goblet cell markers and mucus secretion through hypoxia inducible factor driven mechanisms. Taken together, this pathway appears to represent a colon mucosal barrier and immune interface program rather than a primary cardiac electrophysiologic pathway, with its biological significance residing in regulation of mucus organization, epithelial defense, inflammation, and microbial exposure in the large intestine.

Against this biological background, the available publications do not support a direct mechanistic role of the colonic goblet cell pathway in arrhythmia pathogenesis. Instead, they suggest an indirect and systemic relationship that may be relevant to arrhythmia through inflammation, barrier dysfunction, and hypoxia-associated processes. The strongest evidence indicates that specialized colonic goblet cell populations are essential for maintaining the mucus barrier, and that their depletion or dysfunction exposes the epithelium to microbes and promotes colitis and persistent mucosal inflammation. This point is potentially important because chronic intestinal inflammation and impaired barrier function can contribute to systemic inflammatory signaling, which is a recognized pro-arrhythmic milieu, even though that cardiac connection is not directly tested in these studies. Consistent with this interpretation, goblet cell injury is associated with inflammatory activation involving nuclear factor kappa B, interleukin six, and tumor necrosis factor, as well as oxidative stress pathways, all of which are biologically plausible mediators of atrial and ventricular electrical remodeling in arrhythmia. In addition, excessive mucin production can induce endoplasmic reticulum stress and impair epithelial repair, suggesting that prolonged goblet cell stress may sustain inflammatory barrier failure. A more recent study also demonstrates that hypobaric hypoxia impairs goblet cell subpopulations and mucus secretion through hypoxia inducible factor one alpha signaling, which is noteworthy because hypoxia is itself a known trigger and amplifier of arrhythmic susceptibility. Therefore, the most defensible interpretation is that this pathway is related to arrhythmia only indirectly: altered colonic goblet cell function may promote systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, microbial translocation, and hypoxia-linked stress responses that could secondarily increase arrhythmic risk, but no cited publication demonstrates a direct causal effect on cardiac rhythm disorders.[PubMed:33859001](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33859001) [PubMed:31878169](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31878169) [PubMed:29935164](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29935164) [PubMed:40132123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40132123) [PubMed:33150708](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33150708) 

Consistent with this indirect interpretation, the enrichment results are more suggestive of mucosal defense biology than of a core cardiac rhythm mechanism. There were 21 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in a pathway representing highly expressed goblet cell programs in the colon, centered on mature secretory epithelial cells that synthesize and release mucins to construct the mucus barrier over the colonic surface. This enrichment profile indicates that the identified protein set is functionally concentrated in epithelial barrier biology rather than in a primary cardiac electrophysiologic process, with the pathway description emphasizing goblet cell heterogeneity across the crypt to surface axis, the critical contribution of intercrypt goblet cells to mucus plume organization, and the consequences of goblet cell dysfunction for barrier failure, bacterial encroachment, colitis susceptibility, inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses, endoplasmic reticulum stress, hypoxia responses, and wound repair capacity. In quantitative terms, the analysis is based on 21 proteins, thereby defining a compact but biologically coherent module whose annotated functions converge on mucosal defense, host and microbiota segregation, and immune homeostasis in the large intestine rather than on canonical mechanisms of arrhythmia pathogenesis.

To place this protein set into a network context, the figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 21 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link.
