Building on this network-level overview, the function enrichment analysis identified several proteins that may warrant closer consideration. We introduce them in detail below.

Among the proteins listed, CDH1 stands out because cell-cell adhesion is highly relevant to cardiac electrical stability. Although the provided annotation emphasizes its role in microbial infection rather than canonical epithelial adhesion biology, cadherin-mediated adhesion is fundamentally important for tissue integrity and intercellular coupling. In the heart, disruption of adhesion complexes can alter mechanical continuity and indirectly impair electrical propagation, thereby creating a substrate for arrhythmia. More broadly, remodeling of adhesion systems is a recognized feature of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmogenic disease, where weakened junctional organization can promote conduction heterogeneity and reentry. Thus, even though the supplied function is infection-focused, CDH1 remains one of the more biologically plausible candidates in this list for potential relevance to arrhythmia through mechanisms involving altered cell adhesion and tissue architecture.

Along a different but complementary mechanistic line, CHCHD10 is particularly noteworthy because mitochondrial integrity is central to cardiomyocyte excitability and survival. The heart has exceptionally high energetic demands, and preservation of mitochondrial organization and cristae architecture is required for efficient oxidative phosphorylation, adenosine triphosphate production, and redox balance. Disturbances in these processes can contribute to arrhythmogenesis by impairing ion channel function, calcium handling, and action potential stability. Mitochondrial dysfunction is also closely linked to oxidative stress, which can modify membrane currents and promote triggered activity. Therefore, although the annotation is concise, CHCHD10 has a credible mechanistic connection to arrhythmia through energy failure, abnormal calcium homeostasis, and stress-induced electrical instability in cardiomyocytes.

In addition to adhesion and mitochondrial biology, neural regulatory pathways may also be indirectly relevant. BSG is of potential interest because autonomic neural regulation is an important determinant of cardiac rhythm. The annotated functions of BSG emphasize neuron-glia interactions, axonal maintenance, and regulation of neurite outgrowth, all of which could be relevant indirectly to arrhythmia if altered neural integrity affects sympathetic or parasympathetic control of the heart. Cardiac arrhythmias can be influenced by autonomic imbalance, and proteins involved in neuronal survival and axonal maintenance may contribute to this dimension of disease biology. Although the evidence provided here is neurologically centered rather than cardiac, BSG stands out as a plausible indirect modifier of arrhythmic susceptibility through effects on neural circuitry, neuroprotection, and membrane recognition via ganglioside binding.[PubMed:12089450](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [PubMed:27922006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [PubMed:7533044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [PubMed:10625334](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [PubMed:7516497](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [PubMed:9262180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [PubMed:9469574](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [PubMed:9482781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [PubMed:9482783](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [PubMed:26335717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [PubMed:15953602](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [PubMed:19158290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [PubMed:17640868](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868) 

Extending this discussion from neural regulation to broader remodeling biology, CKAP4 may be relevant to arrhythmia primarily through signaling and structural remodeling pathways. While the supplied annotation is centered on epithelial antiproliferative signaling, receptor-mediated control of proliferation and cellular phenotype can be important in the context of cardiac remodeling. Arrhythmias frequently arise in structurally remodeled myocardium, where fibrosis, altered cell survival, and changes in signaling networks create conduction abnormalities. If CKAP4 participates more broadly in growth-regulatory pathways, it could influence arrhythmia susceptibility indirectly by modulating tissue remodeling rather than acute electrophysiological properties. On the basis of the provided information, this connection remains speculative, but CKAP4 is more relevant than many purely epithelial or secretory proteins in the list because of its receptor and signaling function.

A related consideration applies to proteins involved in cytoskeletal regulation and repair responses. GSN is potentially relevant because proteins that regulate cytoskeletal dynamics and cell state transitions can influence tissue repair and remodeling, both of which are important in arrhythmia pathogenesis. The provided annotation focuses on inhibition of stem cell differentiation and cell-cycle entry, suggesting a role in regulating proliferative responses. In the cardiovascular setting, altered reparative or fibrotic responses after injury can generate arrhythmogenic substrate by disrupting conduction pathways. Although the listed function does not directly implicate cardiomyocytes or ion handling, GSN may still be of interest as a modifier of post-injury remodeling biology, particularly if dysregulation affects cellular turnover or stromal responses that contribute to fibrosis-associated arrhythmia.[PubMed:7694679](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7694679) 

From this perspective of tissue organization, LGALS4 is notable because the assembly of adherens junctions has potential implications for cardiac conduction. In excitable tissues, junctional organization helps maintain structural cohesion and supports proper spatial arrangement of electrical coupling machinery. Defects in adhesion and junctional complexes are well-established contributors to conduction slowing and arrhythmogenic substrate formation. Although LGALS4 is not a canonical cardiac junction protein in the annotation provided, its possible role in adherens junction assembly makes it biologically relevant to arrhythmia, especially in the broader context of tissue architecture, intercellular organization, and disease-associated remodeling.

By comparison, MUC13 appears to have a weaker and more indirect connection to arrhythmia based on the supplied annotation, but it may still merit consideration because transmembrane signaling proteins can influence inflammatory or remodeling pathways. Inflammation and altered signaling are recognized contributors to atrial and ventricular arrhythmogenesis, especially when they promote fibrosis or change cellular stress responses. However, the evidence here is limited and largely nonspecific, so MUC13 should be regarded as a lower-priority candidate compared with proteins linked to adhesion, mitochondrial structure, or neural regulation.

In a somewhat similar indirect manner, RNASE1 is of interest because its annotated roles intersect with two processes relevant to arrhythmia: stress responses and redox homeostasis. Oxidative stress is a major driver of electrical instability in the heart, where it can alter ion channels, gap junctions, calcium cycling, and cell survival. The ability of this protein to participate in redox homeostasis suggests a plausible route by which it could influence arrhythmic risk, particularly under ischemic, inflammatory, or metabolic stress. Its regulation of angiogenin may also be relevant in tissue injury and repair contexts, which can shape arrhythmogenic remodeling. Although the annotation does not establish a direct cardiac role, RNASE1 stands out as a mechanistically credible candidate linking stress biology to arrhythmia susceptibility.[PubMed:12578357](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12578357) [PubMed:14515218](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14515218) [PubMed:3219362](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3219362) [PubMed:3243277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3243277) [PubMed:3470787](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3470787) [PubMed:9050852](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9050852) [PubMed:17292889](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17292889) [PubMed:23843625](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23843625) [PubMed:32510170](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32510170) 

Finally, B3GNT7 is not an obvious arrhythmia gene, but it may have limited indirect relevance through extracellular matrix and tissue architecture. Proteoglycans contribute to matrix organization, and extracellular matrix remodeling is a key determinant of conduction heterogeneity and fibrosis-associated arrhythmia. The annotation also suggests a role in maintenance of tissue architecture, which is conceptually relevant to structural substrates for arrhythmia. Nevertheless, the currently provided evidence is centered on corneal biology and epithelial behavior rather than cardiovascular electrophysiology, so B3GNT7 should be considered a speculative and lower-priority candidate.[PubMed:14706853](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14706853) [PubMed:17690104](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17690104)

### lipid localization (GO:0010876) 

Lipid localization refers to the ensemble of cellular processes that transport lipids to defined membrane domains, organelles, and membrane contact sites, or retain them there once delivered. This pathway is fundamental for membrane identity, membrane fluidity, curvature, signal transduction, ion channel regulation, energy storage, and organelle communication. In cardiomyocytes, lipid localization is especially important because electrical excitability depends on highly organized membrane microdomains at structures such as the intercalated disc, transverse tubules, sarcolemma, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and lipid droplets. Different lipid classes contribute distinct functions: cholesterol shapes membrane order and protein partitioning; phosphatidylinositol four, five-bisphosphate acts as a signaling phospholipid that directly regulates ion channels; phosphatidic acid, lysophosphatidic acid, diacylglycerols, and triglyceride-related intermediates influence membrane composition, metabolism, and stress signaling; and peroxidized phospholipids promote oxidative injury and ferroptotic cell death. Proper localization of these lipids determines whether ion channels, calcium handling proteins, and signaling complexes are correctly targeted and functionally coupled. Conversely, disruption of lipid localization can alter membrane excitability, impair channel trafficking, destabilize conduction, promote oxidative stress, trigger cell death, and remodel the myocardium structurally and electrically. Thus, lipid localization is not merely a metabolic housekeeping process, but may represent a central determinant of cardiac electrophysiological stability.

Building on this biological framework, the collected literature suggests that lipid localization may be mechanistically linked to arrhythmia through several converging levels of cardiac electrophysiology and myocardial integrity. First, spatially restricted membrane lipids directly regulate ion channel behavior and localization. A particularly strong example is the demonstration that fibroblast growth factor thirteen preserves a polarized cholesterol distribution at the intercalated disc in cardiomyocytes; loss of this protein abolishes local cholesterol enrichment, displaces voltage-gated sodium channels from the intercalated disc, and alters steady-state inactivation, thereby providing a direct connection between cholesterol localization, sodium channel organization, and arrhythmogenic conduction disturbance (PubMed:40794434). In parallel, phosphatidylinositol four, five-bisphosphate has been shown to activate small-conductance calcium-activated potassium channel two by binding a critical residue near the channel gate and increasing channel flexibility, supporting the concept that localized phosphoinositide pools tune repolarizing potassium currents that are already recognized as therapeutically relevant in atrial arrhythmia (PubMed:39288178). Second, defective intracellular lipid trafficking and compartmentalization can create a pro-arrhythmic metabolic state. Loss of transport and golgi organization protein two causes abnormal lipid droplet enlargement, disturbed phospholipid and neutral lipid metabolism, increased reactive oxygen species, and lipid peroxidation, and these abnormalities were proposed to help explain the cardiac arrhythmias seen in this genetic disorder (PubMed:36961129). Similarly, high-fat diet-induced cardiac lipotoxicity is accompanied by intracellular lipid droplet accumulation, excess diacylglycerol species, stress kinase activation, calcium handling abnormalities, ectopic activity, and greater vulnerability to ventricular fibrillation, while pharmacological reduction of excess lipid intermediates mitigates these arrhythmic phenotypes, indicating that mislocalized or excessive lipid storage within cardiomyocytes may contribute to electrical instability (PubMed:41124862). Third, lipid peroxidation emerges as an additional bridge between lipid localization and arrhythmia. A recent review of iron overload and ferroptosis emphasizes that membrane lipid peroxide accumulation is a plausible driver of arrhythmia through oxidative injury, altered membrane properties, and cardiomyocyte death (PubMed:38694269). This concept is reinforced by the transport and golgi organization protein two study, in which disturbed lipid homeostasis increased lipid peroxidation together with arrhythmia susceptibility (PubMed:36961129). Fourth, systemic disorders of lipid handling can remodel the heart into an arrhythmogenic substrate. In lean metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis induced by high-fat and high-cholesterol feeding with ethanol exposure, marked cardiac inflammation, fibrosis, and lethal arrhythmias developed, suggesting that chronic abnormalities in lipid distribution and utilization outside and within the heart can secondarily promote structural remodeling that sustains arrhythmia (PubMed:41724180). Although some cited reports concern therapeutic lipid emulsions in toxicological wide-complex arrhythmia rather than endogenous lipid localization biology, they still underscore the sensitivity of cardiac conduction to lipid environments and lipid-based interventions (PubMed:24197589, PubMed:35658706). Taken together, the available evidence supports a coherent model in which lipid localization may influence arrhythmia risk by controlling membrane microdomain composition, ion channel targeting and gating, intracellular lipid droplet and phospholipid homeostasis, oxidative lipid damage, calcium dysregulation, and fibrosis-promoting remodeling.[PubMed:40794434](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40794434) [PubMed:39288178](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39288178) [PubMed:36961129](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36961129) [PubMed:41124862](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41124862) [PubMed:38694269](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38694269) [PubMed:41724180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41724180) [PubMed:24197589](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24197589) [PubMed:35658706](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35658706) 

Consistent with this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment analysis identified 26 arrhythmia-associated proteins in the pathway of lipid localization, a process that governs the transport and retention of lipids across membrane domains, organelles, and membrane contact sites and is therefore highly relevant to the electrophysiological stability of cardiomyocytes. This enrichment is biologically notable because lipid localization directly influences membrane identity, membrane fluidity, curvature, signal transduction, ion channel regulation, energy storage, and inter-organelle communication, all of which are central determinants of normal cardiac conduction and rhythm maintenance. In the context of arrhythmia, the involvement of 26 proteins supports a quantitatively substantial functional module linking lipid handling to electrical excitability, especially at the intercalated disc, transverse tubules, sarcolemma, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and lipid droplets, where mislocalization of cholesterol, phosphatidylinositol four, five-bisphosphate, phosphatidic acid, lysophosphatidic acid, diacylglycerols, triglyceride-related intermediates, and peroxidized phospholipids can disrupt ion channel targeting, calcium coupling, oxidative balance, and structural integrity. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 26 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here: [Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=28D7E01EF5B19ECF).

![PPI Network](imgs/67900f51-0309-48d4-b055-af9b798503b2.png)

With this network-level context in place, the function enrichment analysis further highlighted several proteins that may warrant closer consideration. We introduce them in detail below.

Among the proteins listed, PCSK9 has the clearest and most clinically meaningful connection to arrhythmia, primarily through its major role in lipid metabolism and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. By promoting degradation of low-density lipoprotein receptor and related receptors, PCSK9 increases circulating low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and thereby contributes to coronary artery disease, myocardial ischemia, and infarction, all of which are major structural and electrophysiological substrates for atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. This link is particularly important because ischemic remodeling, fibrosis, and scar formation are well-established mechanisms that promote abnormal impulse generation and re-entry. In addition, PCSK9 may have more direct relevance to cardiac electrophysiology through its inhibition of epithelial sodium channel-mediated sodium absorption and its broader effects on receptor trafficking and proteostasis, although these mechanisms are less well established in the arrhythmia field than its cholesterol-mediated cardiovascular effects. Overall, PCSK9 stands out as the strongest candidate in this list because it connects a well-validated molecular pathway to major upstream causes of arrhythmia, especially ischemic heart disease and adverse cardiac remodeling.[PubMed:18039658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039658) [PubMed:17461796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17461796) [PubMed:18197702](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18197702) [PubMed:18799458](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18799458) [PubMed:22074827](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22074827) [PubMed:18660751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18660751) 

Shifting from lipid-driven ischemic remodeling to immune-mediated remodeling, TREM2 appears highly relevant to arrhythmia because inflammation and innate immune activation are increasingly recognized as major drivers of both atrial and ventricular arrhythmogenesis. Through association with TYROBP and downstream activation pathways, TREM2 regulates immune-cell activation, cytokine production, phagocytosis, and tissue remodeling. Although the provided functional annotations emphasize microglia, dendritic cells, macrophage fusion, and osteoclast biology rather than direct cardiac studies, these same immune signaling principles are highly pertinent to the heart. Inflammatory activation contributes to atrial fibrillation initiation and maintenance by promoting fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, conduction heterogeneity, and altered ion-channel expression. Likewise, post-injury inflammatory responses after myocardial infarction can facilitate ventricular arrhythmias. The annotations showing that TREM2-TYROBP signaling promotes pro-inflammatory responses, regulates interleukin ten and interleukin one receptor-associated kinase three, supports phagocytosis, and affects survival and maturation of immune cells suggest that this axis could influence the balance between reparative and maladaptive cardiac inflammation. Therefore, TREM2 stands out as an indirect but potentially important arrhythmia-related protein through immune and remodeling mechanisms.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) 

In a related but more upstream regulatory context, PSAP is of potential interest in arrhythmia because abnormal ribonucleic acid splicing, transcriptional repression, and apoptosis are important mechanisms in cardiac remodeling and electrical instability. The most relevant feature here is its role in splicing modulation of BCL2L1 and Bcl-X and its association with apoptosis-related regulatory complexes. Cardiomyocyte apoptosis contributes to structural remodeling, fibrosis, and impaired electrical coupling, all of which can facilitate arrhythmia. In addition, alternative splicing has a recognized role in controlling cardiac ion channels, calcium-handling proteins, and structural proteins; therefore, proteins involved in spliceosomal and exon junction complex biology may influence arrhythmic susceptibility even if a direct cardiac role is not specified in the current annotation. PSAP is thus not a primary arrhythmia gene, but it stands out as a plausible upstream regulator of disease mechanisms relevant to arrhythmogenesis, particularly through apoptosis and post-transcriptional gene regulation.

Extending this logic to proteins with more indirect cardiometabolic relevance, PRAP1 has a possible but comparatively weaker connection to arrhythmia. Its most relevant feature is its role in lipid handling through facilitation of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein-mediated lipid transfer and apolipoprotein B lipoprotein assembly, which could theoretically influence systemic lipid profiles and thereby affect long-term cardiovascular risk. Since dyslipidemia contributes to coronary artery disease and ischemic remodeling, PRAP1 may have an indirect relationship to arrhythmia similar in principle, though likely much less prominent, than PCSK9. Its additional functions in apoptosis resistance and p53-dependent survival suggest a broader role in stress responses, but the annotations are centered on gastrointestinal and epithelial biology rather than myocardium or cardiac conduction tissue. Thus, PRAP1 may be considered a secondary candidate with indirect relevance through cardiometabolic disease mechanisms rather than direct arrhythmogenic pathways.[PubMed:14583459](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14583459) [PubMed:23235459](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23235459) [PubMed:24374861](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24374861) 

Moving further toward proteins with only limited inferred relevance, RBP2 has only an indirect potential relationship to arrhythmia based on the provided annotation. Retinoid signaling is important in development, differentiation, and transcriptional regulation, including in the cardiovascular system, but the present functional description is restricted to intracellular retinol transport and does not provide direct evidence for a role in cardiac electrophysiology or arrhythmia. Any connection would therefore be speculative and likely mediated through broader effects of vitamin A metabolism on tissue homeostasis rather than a specific arrhythmogenic mechanism.

Along the same lines, RBP5 has no strong direct link to arrhythmia in the provided functional annotation. Its role in intracellular retinol transport may be relevant to general cellular differentiation and transcriptional programs, but there is insufficient evidence here to prioritize it as an arrhythmia-related protein. At most, it may have a distant connection through systemic retinoid biology rather than through known mechanisms of cardiac conduction, ion-channel regulation, fibrosis, or myocardial injury.

Finally, RBP7 is another retinol-transport protein with only a tenuous inferred connection to arrhythmia from the current information. Because retinoid pathways can influence vascular and metabolic biology, one could hypothesize indirect cardiovascular effects, but the annotation does not support a specific role in electrophysiological remodeling or arrhythmia pathogenesis. Accordingly, RBP7 is not a leading candidate in this set for arrhythmia relevance.

### late endosome (GO:0005770) 

The late endosome is a prelysosomal compartment of the endocytic system that arises during maturation from the early endosome and is characterized by progressive acidification, altered membrane lipid composition, changes in associated small guanosine triphosphatases and sorting complexes, and a predominantly juxtanuclear localization. Functionally, the late endosome serves as a major decision-making station for intracellular cargo, where internalized membrane proteins, receptors, lipids, and signaling complexes are either directed toward lysosomal degradation, recycled through retrieval pathways, or transferred through membrane contact sites to other organelles. Several cited studies define core mechanisms of late endosome biology. Sorting nexin twenty-seven together with the retromer complex prevents angiotensin converting enzyme two cargo from progressing toward lysosome and late endosome compartments, illustrating the importance of retrieval pathways in controlling receptor fate and membrane homeostasis (PubMed:35022217). Programmed cell death six interacting protein and the autophagy machinery component autophagy related twelve to autophagy related three regulate late endosome distribution, endolysosomal trafficking, exosome biogenesis, and basal autophagic flux, demonstrating that late endosome function is tightly integrated with membrane quality control pathways (PubMed:25686249). Programmed cell death protein eight interacts with Ras related protein Rab seven and protrudin at endoplasmic reticulum to late endosome membrane contact sites, where mitochondria can also be recruited, indicating that the late endosome participates in interorganelle communication and lipid transfer (PubMed:32686675; PubMed:34552186). Additional studies show that phosphoinositide remodeling, adaptor protein complex mediated retrieval, and Rab seven dependent positioning govern late endosome maturation, cargo sorting, and spatial distribution (PubMed:34035258; PubMed:29381698; PubMed:30012887; PubMed:26783301). The lipid environment of the late endosome is also biologically important, especially bis monoacylglycero phosphate, which influences late endosome morphology, cholesterol handling, and membrane fusion properties (PubMed:36823305). Overall, this pathway encompasses endosome maturation, cargo sorting, organelle positioning, membrane contact formation, autophagy related trafficking, and lipid homeostasis, all of which may be relevant to excitable tissues such as the heart.

Against this mechanistic background, the available literature supports an indirect but biologically plausible connection between late endosome dysfunction and arrhythmia through processes central to cardiomyocyte homeostasis, membrane receptor turnover, lipid handling, autophagy, and organelle communication, even though only one cited study addresses recurrent atrial arrhythmia clinically and does so in the distinct context of late gadolinium enhancement magnetic resonance imaging rather than late endosome biology (PubMed:31422685). In mechanistic terms, late endosomes regulate whether membrane proteins are recycled or degraded, and this is highly relevant in the cardiac setting because arrhythmia often emerges from altered abundance or localization of ion channels, transporters, and signaling receptors at the cell surface. The study showing that sorting nexin twenty-seven and the retromer complex control the trafficking fate of angiotensin converting enzyme two by preventing its progression into lysosome and late endosome compartments is notable because angiotensin converting enzyme two is a key component of the renin angiotensin system, a pathway strongly implicated in electrical remodeling, fibrosis, and susceptibility to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias; thus, disturbed late endosomal sorting could modify angiotensin converting enzyme two availability and downstream profibrotic or proarrhythmic signaling (PubMed:35022217). Late endosome function is also linked to basal autophagic flux through the interaction of autophagy related twelve to autophagy related three with programmed cell death six interacting protein, and impairment of this axis causes perinuclear accumulation of late endosomes and defective endolysosomal trafficking (PubMed:25686249). Because defective autophagy and lysosome associated degradation in cardiomyocytes promote accumulation of damaged proteins and organelles, calcium handling abnormalities, and structural remodeling, this observation provides a credible route by which late endosome dysfunction could contribute to arrhythmogenic substrate formation. The studies on programmed cell death protein eight, protrudin, and Ras related protein Rab seven further show that late endosomes form membrane contact sites with the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, integrating lipid transport and organelle dynamics (PubMed:32686675; PubMed:34552186). In the heart, abnormal communication among sarcoplasmic reticulum equivalent structures, mitochondria, and endolysosomal compartments can disturb calcium cycling and energetic balance, both of which are central determinants of triggered activity and conduction instability. Lipid composition of the late endosome is another potentially important link. Lysosomal phospholipase A two regulates production of bis monoacylglycero phosphate, and altered levels affect late endosome and lysosome morphology as well as cholesterol accumulation (PubMed:36823305). This is relevant because membrane lipid imbalance can alter ion channel function and trafficking, while the antiarrhythmic drug amiodarone itself was shown to impair trafficking through late endosomes and induce a Niemann Pick disease type C like phenotype with lipid accumulation and disrupted late endocytic processing (PubMed:21878321). This observation suggests that part of the cellular toxicity profile of antiarrhythmic therapy may involve late endosome and lysosome dysfunction. Collectively, the cited studies indicate that the late endosome pathway is not yet an established canonical arrhythmia pathway, but it is mechanistically connected to several upstream determinants of arrhythmogenesis, including renin angiotensin signaling, receptor and membrane protein turnover, autophagic quality control, interorganelle calcium and metabolic coupling, and drug induced lipid trafficking defects, thereby making late endosome biology a plausible contributor to arrhythmia susceptibility and progression.[PubMed:35022217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35022217) [PubMed:32686675](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32686675) [PubMed:25686249](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25686249) [PubMed:34035258](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34035258) [PubMed:34552186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34552186) [PubMed:30012887](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30012887) [PubMed:29381698](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29381698) [PubMed:26783301](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26783301) [PubMed:36823305](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36823305) [PubMed:21878321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21878321) [PubMed:31422685](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31422685) 

Consistent with this mechanistic interpretation, the enrichment results suggest that the pathway captures a focused but biologically substantial signal within the broader arrhythmia associated protein set.

There were 16 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing the late endosome as a prelysosomal compartment of the endocytic system, indicating a focused but biologically substantial signal centered on endosome maturation, progressive acidification, membrane lipid remodeling, cargo sorting, juxtanuclear positioning, membrane contact formation, autophagy-related trafficking, and lipid homeostasis. This enrichment is notable because the pathway integrates several quantitatively important cellular decision points, including the routing of internalized membrane proteins, receptors, lipids, and signaling complexes either toward lysosomal degradation or toward retrieval and recycling pathways, with direct implications for membrane composition and signaling control in excitable cardiac tissue. The pathway description further highlights specific mechanistic modules supported by published evidence, including sorting nexin twenty-seven and the retromer complex in preventing angiotensin converting enzyme two cargo progression toward lysosome and late endosome compartments (PubMed:35022217), programmed cell death six interacting protein together with autophagy related twelve to autophagy related three in regulating late endosome distribution, endolysosomal trafficking, exosome biogenesis, and basal autophagic flux (PubMed:25686249), programmed cell death protein eight with Ras related protein Rab seven and protrudin at endoplasmic reticulum to late endosome membrane contact sites that can additionally recruit mitochondria (PubMed:32686675; PubMed:34552186), and phosphoinositide remodeling, adaptor protein complex mediated retrieval, and Rab seven dependent positioning in governing maturation, cargo sorting, and spatial distribution (PubMed:34035258; PubMed:29381698; PubMed:30012887; PubMed:26783301). The biological scope of the enrichment is further strengthened by the role of bis monoacylglycero phosphate in controlling late endosome morphology, cholesterol handling, and membrane fusion properties (PubMed:36823305), thereby connecting this 16-protein signal to multiple quantitatively distinct trafficking and membrane regulatory processes that may contribute to arrhythmia through altered receptor turnover, intracellular signaling persistence, organelle communication, and lipid-dependent membrane behavior.

Having outlined the pathway-level signal and its interaction architecture, the following section introduces several of the significant proteins in greater detail.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
Among the listed proteins, EGFR stands out as one of the most plausibly connected to arrhythmia because dysregulated receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, SRC activation, and MAPK pathway engagement are all highly relevant to cardiac remodeling, electrical instability, and stress-responsive signaling in the myocardium. The described function indicates that EGFR not only transduces growth factor signals but also directly regulates their amplitude and duration through ubiquitin-dependent turnover of EGFR itself, as well as SRC phosphorylated at Tyr-419. This is important because excessive EGFR/SRC/MAPK signaling has been implicated in maladaptive hypertrophy, fibrosis, and altered ion-channel regulation, each of which can create a substrate for atrial or ventricular arrhythmias. In addition, the ability of one EGFR isoform to inhibit EGF-stimulated MAPK1 activation suggests isoform-specific control of signaling intensity, which may influence disease susceptibility or progression. Although the provided annotation does not explicitly mention cardiac tissue, the combination of ubiquitin-mediated receptor control and canonical pro-remodeling signaling makes EGFR one of the most mechanistically relevant proteins in relation to arrhythmogenesis.

In a related but more systemic manner, PCSK9 may also be relevant to arrhythmia through its effects on lipid metabolism and receptor degradation.

PCSK9 is highly relevant to arrhythmia primarily through its central role in lipid metabolism and receptor degradation. Its promotion of LDLR degradation is a major determinant of circulating LDL cholesterol levels, and this is clinically important because dyslipidemia contributes to coronary artery disease and ischemic heart disease, which are major upstream causes of both atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. Thus, even if PCSK9 is not a classical ion-channel gene, it is strongly connected to arrhythmia through cardiovascular disease mechanisms that alter myocardial perfusion, promote scar formation, and create electrophysiological heterogeneity. The annotation also notes effects on autophagy/lysosomal pathways and ENaC surface expression, suggesting broader roles in membrane protein turnover and cellular homeostasis. These proteostatic functions may be relevant in the stressed heart, where altered receptor trafficking and degradation can influence remodeling. Therefore, PCSK9 stands out because it links systemic cardiometabolic risk with intracellular degradation pathways, both of which can contribute to arrhythmia susceptibility.[PubMed:18039658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039658) [PubMed:17461796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17461796) [PubMed:18197702](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18197702) [PubMed:18799458](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18799458) [PubMed:22074827](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22074827) [PubMed:18660751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18660751) 

Extending this theme from receptor and lipid turnover to intracellular quality control, LAMP3 may be of interest because of its roles in proteostasis and autophagy.

LAMP3 is notable because impaired proteostasis and autophagy are increasingly recognized as important contributors to cardiac remodeling and arrhythmia. The protein is described as participating in the unfolded protein response and in lysosome-autophagosome fusion, two processes that are essential for removal of damaged proteins and organelles. In cardiomyocytes, failure of these quality-control pathways can lead to accumulation of misfolded proteins, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular stress, and ultimately structural and electrical remodeling that predisposes to arrhythmia. Its role in supporting cell survival during proteasomal dysfunction is particularly relevant in the heart, where chronic stress conditions such as ischemia, hypertrophy, and heart failure impose a high burden on protein quality-control systems. In addition, activation of PI3K/Akt signaling may influence survival and remodeling responses. Although the annotation does not directly connect LAMP3 to electrophysiology, its functions align closely with disease mechanisms that can facilitate arrhythmogenesis through myocardial stress adaptation and maladaptive remodeling.

A further extension of this framework involves inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways, which brings IL12B into consideration.

IL12B is of interest in the arrhythmia context because it integrates three processes that are highly relevant to myocardial disease: autophagy, inflammation, and oxidative stress. The annotation indicates that it functions as a ubiquitin-binding autophagy adapter, regulates type I interferon signaling, and promotes activation of the KEAP1-NRF2 antioxidant pathway during oxidative stress. These pathways are important because atrial and ventricular arrhythmias often arise in tissue exposed to chronic inflammatory signaling, redox imbalance, and defective protein turnover. Oxidative stress can alter ion-channel function and calcium handling, whereas inflammatory signaling promotes fibrosis and electrical heterogeneity. By influencing selective autophagy and antioxidant defense, this protein could affect how cardiomyocytes or immune cells respond to stress and injury. Its role in IL-12 trafficking also suggests an immunomodulatory function that may indirectly shape arrhythmogenic remodeling, especially in inflammatory or systemic disease states.[PubMed:31916398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31916398) [PubMed:34374750](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34374750) 

Along similar lines, BST2 may be considered in the context of immune activation, antiviral defense, and matrix remodeling.

BST2 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because it links antiviral defense, interferon signaling, NF-kappa-B activation, matrix-related protease regulation, and cytoskeletal organization. These functions are noteworthy in the setting of arrhythmias associated with viral myocarditis or inflammatory cardiomyopathy, where interferon-driven immune responses and NF-kappa-B signaling can contribute to myocardial injury and electrical instability. The ability of BST2 to modulate plasmacytoid dendritic cell interferon production suggests a role in shaping the intensity of antiviral inflammation, which may influence the extent of myocardial inflammation and subsequent arrhythmogenic remodeling. Its inhibition of MMP14/MMP15-related growth and migration is also potentially important, because matrix remodeling and fibrosis are central determinants of conduction abnormalities. While BST2 is not a canonical arrhythmia gene, its immune and remodeling-related functions make it a plausible modifier in infection-associated or inflammation-associated arrhythmic disease.[PubMed:18200009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [PubMed:18342597](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [PubMed:19036818](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [PubMed:19879838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [PubMed:20019814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [PubMed:20399176](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [PubMed:20419159](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [PubMed:20940320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [PubMed:21529378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [PubMed:22520941](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [PubMed:19179289](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19179289) [PubMed:20686043](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20686043) [PubMed:20943977](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20943977) [PubMed:21621240](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21621240) [PubMed:26378163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26378163) [PubMed:31199522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31199522) [PubMed:22065321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [PubMed:19564354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [PubMed:26172439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [PubMed:23028328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328) 

Moving from inflammatory regulation to signaling turnover, RNF149 may represent a more indirect pathway-level candidate.

RNF149 is a plausible, though more indirect, candidate of interest because it regulates BRAF stability. BRAF is a central component of the MAPK signaling cascade, and aberrant MAPK pathway activation is strongly linked to cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and remodeling, all of which can create an arrhythmogenic substrate. Through ubiquitin-mediated degradation of BRAF, RNF149 may act as a brake on pro-growth and stress signaling. In principle, altered RNF149 activity could influence downstream ERK signaling and thereby affect structural remodeling of the myocardium. Although the evidence provided here is limited to a single biochemical function and does not directly address cardiac biology, this pathway-level connection makes RNF149 relevant as a potential modifier of arrhythmia susceptibility.

Finally, VAMP5 may have a weaker but still potentially meaningful connection through vesicular trafficking and metabolic regulation in muscle.

VAMP5 has a weaker but still potentially meaningful connection to arrhythmia through membrane trafficking and muscle biology. Its proposed role in myogenesis and GLUT4 trafficking suggests involvement in vesicular transport processes that are broadly important for excitable tissues. In the heart, disturbances in membrane trafficking can affect the localization of channels, transporters, and metabolic regulators, thereby influencing electrical stability and energetic state. The GLUT4-related aspect is particularly relevant because metabolic dysfunction and insulin resistance are associated with atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias. However, compared with EGFR, PCSK9, LAMP3, or IL12B, the current annotation provides only a limited and indirect basis for implicating VAMP5 in arrhythmia mechanisms.

### ruffle membrane (GO:0032587) 

Ruffle membrane refers to the portion of the plasma membrane that surrounds membrane ruffles, which are highly dynamic, actin-supported protrusive structures generated by localized remodeling of the cell cortex. These structures include peripheral ruffles and circular dorsal ruffles, and they are typically induced by growth factor signaling, small guanosine triphosphatase activation, phosphoinositide remodeling, phosphatidic acid production, and changes in membrane tension. The ruffle membrane serves as a specialized platform for signal transduction, membrane trafficking, receptor internalization, mechanosensing, and macropinocytosis. Several studies show that recruitment of signaling and trafficking proteins to ruffle membrane domains depends on coordinated actin polymerization and lipid patterning. For example, dedicator of cytokinesis 1 is selectively recruited to dorsal ruffles through phosphatidic acid, thereby promoting ruffle formation, while inositol polyphosphate five phosphatase proteins are also targeted to membrane ruffles through dedicated localization domains. More broadly, membrane ruffles can concentrate ion channels, signaling proteins, and secretory machinery, and can convert mechanical membrane deformation into calcium entry and downstream signaling. Although this pathway has been studied mainly in cancer, infection, and immune cell biology, its core biological themes, namely membrane shaping, actin-dependent compartmentalization, mechanosensitive signaling, and control of local ion movement, may also be relevant to excitable tissues such as the heart. In cardiomyocytes, closely related membrane specializations of the surface membrane and transverse tubular system regulate extracellular microdomains, ion channel localization, and excitation-contraction coupling, suggesting that abnormal membrane folding or loss of protective membrane architecture could have direct electrophysiological consequences.

With this cellular framework in mind, the potential relationship between ruffle membrane biology and arrhythmia appears indirect but biologically meaningful, because the central processes governed by ruffle membranes, namely actin-driven plasma membrane remodeling, local control of ion flux, mechanosensitive signaling, and membrane organization, overlap with mechanisms that contribute to cardiac electrical stability. The strongest arrhythmia-relevant evidence among the provided studies comes from work showing that bridging integrator 1 maintains folded membrane architecture within cardiomyocyte transverse tubules; when this membrane folding is reduced, local extracellular calcium and potassium diffusion becomes less restricted, action potential duration is prolonged, and susceptibility to ventricular arrhythmias increases, demonstrating that specialized membrane topologies may protect against arrhythmogenesis by controlling ion microenvironments (PubMed:24836577). This concept is further supported by evidence that the cardiac sodium channel is differentially organized across cardiomyocyte membrane domains, including the lateral membrane and transverse tubules, and that altered membrane-domain targeting redistributes channel clusters in ways that may contribute to arrhythmic phenotypes (PubMed:32536203). In addition, other publications support the mechanistic plausibility that ruffle membrane-associated signaling could influence electrophysiology through membrane mechanics and ion entry. For example, infection-induced membrane ruffling activates piezo type mechanosensitive ion channel component 1, causing calcium influx and adenosine triphosphate release, which illustrates how membrane deformation at ruffled plasma membrane regions can be converted into ion-dependent signaling events (PubMed:35947957). Furthermore, general studies of membrane ruffles show that these structures are organized by rac family small guanosine triphosphatase 1, phosphatidic acid, phospholipase D, and phosphoinositide regulators, which are molecular systems capable of reshaping membrane architecture and thereby altering local signaling and trafficking environments (PubMed:23362269, PubMed:12536145, PubMed:31391241, PubMed:39456754). Although no publication provided here demonstrates that the ruffle membrane itself is a primary canonical arrhythmia pathway, the collective evidence suggests that disruption of ruffle-like membrane remodeling and membrane-folding programs could promote arrhythmia by disturbing ion channel localization, extracellular ion buffering, mechanosensitive calcium signaling, and action potential repolarization. This overall framework is compatible with established arrhythmia mechanisms involving reduced repolarizing potassium current, altered sodium channel distribution, and abnormal calcium handling, as illustrated by studies of potassium channel dysfunction in inherited and drug-provoked arrhythmia and by disease models showing that altered membrane electrophysiology and calcium homeostasis increase atrial and ventricular arrhythmic vulnerability (PubMed:10219239, PubMed:40557493).[PubMed:24836577](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24836577) [PubMed:32536203](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32536203) [PubMed:35947957](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35947957) [PubMed:23362269](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23362269) [PubMed:12536145](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12536145) [PubMed:31391241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31391241) [PubMed:39456754](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39456754) [PubMed:10219239](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10219239) [PubMed:40557493](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40557493) 

Building on this biological rationale, the enrichment result provides a quantitative indication that this membrane-centered process may intersect with arrhythmia-related biology.

There were 6 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of ruffle membrane. This enrichment highlights a membrane-centered biological theme in which localized plasma membrane remodeling, actin-supported protrusion formation, receptor trafficking, mechanosensitive signaling, and local ion movement converge within specialized surface domains. Although the pathway annotation has been characterized primarily in cancer, infection, and immune cell systems, its underlying cellular architecture may still be relevant to cardiac electrophysiology because excitable cardiac cells depend on finely organized membrane microdomains to control ion channel positioning, extracellular compartment geometry, calcium entry, and excitation-contraction coupling. In this context, an enrichment supported by 6 disease-associated proteins suggests that a measurable subset of the arrhythmia-related protein set maps to processes involving membrane shaping and cortical actin coordination, thereby providing a plausible mechanistic link between altered membrane structure and abnormal electrical activity.

To further contextualize these 6 proteins, the interaction map below illustrates how they are connected at the protein network level, which may help guide interpretation of their potential functional convergence.

Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 6 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct inspection of the evidence-supported interaction map.

![PPI Network](imgs/4df2b68f-e48b-4f97-a93d-50539ffd8d20.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=9301317A96E8EE3C)

Following this network-level overview, the individual proteins identified in the enrichment analysis can be considered in greater detail with respect to their possible relevance to arrhythmia-related mechanisms.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the proteins listed, EPS8L2 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because its annotated functions converge on actin cytoskeletal remodeling and son of sevenless homolog 1-associated signaling. Although the provided functional description is centered on membrane dynamics and cochlear stereocilia maintenance rather than the heart directly, cytoskeletal organization is highly relevant to cardiac electrophysiology. In cardiomyocytes, the actin cytoskeleton contributes to membrane stability, ion-channel localization, intercalated disc integrity, and mechano-electric coupling; disruption of these processes can create a substrate for conduction abnormalities and arrhythmogenesis. The link to son of sevenless homolog 1 is also noteworthy because son of sevenless homolog 1 participates in rat sarcoma virus and mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, a pathway implicated in structural and electrical cardiac remodeling in several inherited and acquired cardiac disorders. Therefore, EPS8L2 may be considered a plausible indirect arrhythmia-relevant candidate, particularly in mechanisms involving cytoskeletal disorganization or signaling-dependent remodeling, although the current annotation does not establish a direct causal role in arrhythmia.

In a related but somewhat more membrane-trafficking-centered context, HIP1R appears to have a comparatively stronger mechanistic connection to arrhythmia-relevant cellular processes.

HIP1R stands out as one of the more compelling arrhythmia-relevant proteins in this set because it integrates endocytosis, phosphoinositide binding, actin cytoskeletal interactions, and receptor tyrosine kinase stabilization. These functions may be important in the heart, where regulated membrane trafficking governs the surface abundance and turnover of ion channels, transporters, and signaling receptors that determine excitability and conduction. Abnormal endocytic trafficking can alter the localization of sodium, calcium, or potassium channels, thereby predisposing to repolarization defects, triggered activity, or conduction slowing. In addition, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling influences cardiomyocyte survival, hypertrophic remodeling, and fibrosis, all of which can secondarily generate an arrhythmogenic substrate. By linking clathrin-mediated endocytosis to the actin cytoskeleton, HIP1R may participate in the dynamic control of membrane protein composition and stress responses in excitable cells. Thus, while not a canonical arrhythmia gene, HIP1R has a biologically meaningful connection to disease mechanisms that may promote arrhythmia through altered channel trafficking and maladaptive remodeling.

A third protein of interest, FAP, appears to connect to arrhythmia more indirectly through tissue remodeling processes rather than through direct regulation of membrane excitability.

FAP is of possible interest in arrhythmia primarily through extracellular proteolytic regulation rather than direct electrophysiological effects. Protease activity and its inhibition influence extracellular matrix turnover, tissue remodeling, inflammation, and fibrosis, all of which are central determinants of arrhythmogenic substrate formation, especially in atrial and ventricular remodeling. In particular, modulation of plasmin-related proteolysis could affect matrix degradation and reparative responses after injury, with downstream consequences for conduction heterogeneity. However, compared with EPS8L2 and HIP1R, the connection of FAP to arrhythmia is more indirect based on the provided annotation alone. Its relevance would likely be strongest in contexts where abnormal protease balance contributes to fibrotic remodeling, scar formation, or structural heart disease that subsequently predisposes to arrhythmia.

### collagen metabolic process (GO:0032963) 

The collagen metabolic process comprises the synthesis, post-translational modification, secretion, assembly, cross-linking, turnover, and degradation of collagen, the principal tensile element of the extracellular matrix in connective tissues. In the heart, collagen is produced predominantly by fibroblasts and myofibroblasts and is essential for maintaining myocardial architecture, mechanical integrity, force transmission, and the spatial organization of cardiomyocytes, blood vessels, and specialized conduction tissue. This pathway includes transcription of collagen genes, intracellular processing of procollagen, hydroxylation of key amino acid residues such as lysine and proline, extracellular fibril formation, and continuous remodeling through the coordinated actions of matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors. Physiologically, balanced collagen metabolism preserves tissue compliance and supports normal electrical coupling by maintaining appropriate interstitial structure. Pathologically, either excessive collagen deposition or defective collagen synthesis and extracellular matrix maintenance can disrupt cardiac function. Increased collagen accumulation promotes fibrosis, tissue stiffening, fibroblast activation, and architectural disorganization, whereas impaired collagen synthesis or extracellular matrix depletion can weaken tissue structure and alter cell-matrix signaling. Because impulse generation and propagation in the heart depend on the integrity of the tissue scaffold surrounding cardiomyocytes and pacemaker regions, disturbances in collagen metabolism can directly influence conduction velocity, anisotropy, calcium handling, and susceptibility to both atrial and ventricular arrhythmias.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that dysregulation of the collagen metabolic process is closely linked to arrhythmia because abnormal collagen synthesis and remodeling may create a structural substrate that destabilizes cardiac impulse formation and propagation. Multiple studies support a model in which increased collagen deposition and fibrosis promote arrhythmogenesis by separating cardiomyocyte bundles, increasing conduction heterogeneity, and coupling structural remodeling to ion-channel dysregulation. Human myocardial transcriptomic analysis at sudden cardiac death showed that arrhythmic deaths were strongly enriched for genes related to the collagen-containing extracellular matrix and fibrosis, including elevated expression of collagen-associated markers and activated fibroblast signatures, indicating that active fibrotic remodeling may represent a vulnerable substrate for lethal arrhythmias rather than merely a chronic bystander lesion (PubMed:39545913). Consistently, experimental studies in pacing-induced heart failure and in premature ventricular contraction-induced cardiomyopathy demonstrated that increased collagen synthesis, fibroblast expansion, and interstitial collagen accumulation accompany heightened ventricular arrhythmia susceptibility, whereas interventions that suppress fibroblast proliferation and collagen production reduce fibrosis and improve arrhythmic outcomes (PubMed:40220080, PubMed:41527819). The relevance extends beyond ventricular myocardium to specialized pacemaker tissue, where fibrosis of the sinoatrial node impairs pacemaker function; notably, targeted vesicle therapy that reduced fibrotic remodeling in the sinoatrial node restored intrinsic pacemaking in preclinical sinus node dysfunction models, directly connecting excess collagen-rich matrix to rhythm disturbance (PubMed:41365863). Likewise, sex-specific transcriptomic profiling of the human sinoatrial node found enrichment of collagen biosynthetic and fibrogenic pathways in males, suggesting that heightened collagen metabolic activity in conduction tissue may contribute to susceptibility to conduction impairment and atrial fibrillation (PubMed:40265247). Additional support comes from metabolic and inflammatory disease contexts in which collagen accumulation appears mechanistically upstream of arrhythmia: atrial fibrillation reviews consistently identify transforming growth factor beta one-driven collagen deposition as a central determinant of atrial structural remodeling, while experimental work suggests oxidative injury and ferroptotic lipid products may worsen atrial fibrillation in part by inhibiting collagen degradation and thereby intensifying fibrosis (PubMed:36155200, PubMed:39940048). Importantly, disruption of collagen metabolism does not have to involve collagen excess alone; in zebrafish, toxicant-induced inhibition of extracellular matrix production and collagen synthesis persisted after exposure cessation and was accompanied by worsened arrhythmia and disturbed calcium homeostasis, implying that inadequate collagen synthesis and defective matrix maintenance can also destabilize the electromechanical environment required for normal rhythm (PubMed:39299332). Finally, biomaterial evidence reinforces the possible causal importance of the collagen matrix itself: an electrically conductive collagen-based hydrogel improved calcium handling, conduction, and reduced post-infarction ventricular tachycardia, suggesting that restoration of a functionally supportive collagen microenvironment may be antiarrhythmic (PubMed:38653478). Taken together, these studies suggest that the collagen metabolic process is related to arrhythmia through both excessive fibrotic collagen accumulation and defective collagen-extracellular matrix homeostasis, each of which may remodel the myocardial substrate in ways that favor abnormal automaticity, conduction disturbance, reentry, and lethal rhythm disorders.[PubMed:39545913](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39545913) [PubMed:40220080](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40220080) [PubMed:41527819](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41527819) [PubMed:41365863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41365863) [PubMed:40265247](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40265247) [PubMed:36155200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36155200) [PubMed:39940048](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39940048) [PubMed:39299332](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39299332) [PubMed:38653478](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38653478) 

Building on this literature context, the enrichment results provide a more focused view of the specific proteins that may connect this pathway to arrhythmia biology. There were 14 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the collagen metabolic process, a pathway that encompasses collagen synthesis, post-translational modification, secretion, fibril assembly, cross-linking, turnover, and degradation within the cardiac extracellular matrix. This enrichment highlights a quantitatively focused set of 14 proteins linked to a structural program that is highly relevant to arrhythmia biology, because even modest disruption of collagen homeostasis can alter myocardial architecture, tissue stiffness, conduction pathways, and the spatial organization of cardiomyocytes and specialized conduction tissue, thereby increasing susceptibility to both atrial and ventricular rhythm disturbances. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 14 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/b824e454-7ffe-4f77-b450-18db60e1414e.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=7535317095C5B1D6)

To further connect the enrichment signal with potential biological interpretation, the significant proteins identified in this analysis are introduced below in a more detailed and sequential manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

COL5A1 is notable in the context of arrhythmia because it participates in extracellular matrix organization, a process that is highly relevant to myocardial structural remodeling. Although type V collagen is a quantitatively minor collagen, it regulates fibrillogenesis and matrix architecture, which can influence myocardial stiffness, cell–matrix signaling, and the development of interstitial fibrosis. Cardiac fibrosis is a well-established substrate for conduction heterogeneity, slowed impulse propagation, and re-entry, thereby increasing susceptibility to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. The reported binding of type V collagen to heparan sulfate and thrombospondin further suggests potential involvement in matrix signaling networks that modulate fibroblast activation and tissue repair. Thus, COL5A1 stands out primarily as a plausible contributor to arrhythmia through structural remodeling rather than direct electrophysiological effects.  

In a related manner, the next protein may also be relevant through its influence on extracellular matrix turnover rather than through a direct effect on cardiac electrophysiology. FAP is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because inhibition of plasmin and related proteases may alter extracellular matrix turnover, proteolytic signaling, and tissue remodeling. In the heart, balanced protease activity is required for normal repair after injury; excessive or insufficient proteolysis can promote maladaptive fibrosis, inflammation, and scar formation, all of which are recognized arrhythmogenic substrates. By restraining plasmin-dependent proteolysis, FAP could influence the extent of matrix degradation and the activation of downstream remodeling cascades. Although the evidence linking this specific inhibitor directly to arrhythmia is likely indirect, its functional position in protease regulation makes it mechanistically relevant to fibrotic remodeling and conduction abnormalities.  

Along similar lines, MFAP4 appears to fit within the broader theme of matrix-dependent structural remodeling. MFAP4 is of interest for arrhythmia because it may influence cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions as well as elastic fiber integrity, both of which are important determinants of myocardial mechanical properties and structural coupling. Abnormal extracellular microfibril and elastic fiber organization can contribute to adverse cardiac remodeling, chamber dilation, and altered mechano-electric feedback. In atrial and ventricular myocardium, disturbances in tissue architecture can disrupt uniform impulse propagation and facilitate arrhythmogenic conduction patterns. The suggested calcium-dependent adhesive function is also conceptually relevant, as calcium handling and calcium-sensitive intercellular interactions are central to cardiac excitation–contraction coupling and arrhythmia susceptibility. Therefore, MFAP4 stands out as a candidate matrix-associated modulator of structural arrhythmogenic remodeling.  

Among the listed proteins, MMP8 may represent one of the more direct mechanistic links to collagen remodeling itself. MMP8 is the most directly compelling protein in this list with respect to arrhythmia because it is a collagen-degrading matrix metalloproteinase capable of remodeling the fibrillar collagen network. The balance between collagen deposition and degradation is a central determinant of cardiac fibrosis, scar maturation, and extracellular matrix integrity. Excessive or dysregulated collagen turnover can create heterogeneous conduction pathways, alter tissue anisotropy, and promote both atrial and ventricular re-entry. Because type I and III collagens are major components of the cardiac interstitium, MMP8-mediated remodeling could influence myocardial stiffness, fibroblast activity, and electrical discontinuity. In disease settings such as myocardial infarction, heart failure, or atrial remodeling, altered matrix metalloproteinase activity has been repeatedly implicated in the generation of arrhythmogenic substrate. Accordingly, MMP8 stands out as a strong mechanistic link between extracellular matrix remodeling and arrhythmia risk.  

By contrast, the final protein currently remains difficult to interpret within the available evidence base. PRSS2 cannot be meaningfully prioritized for arrhythmia relevance based on the current input because no functional annotation was provided. Without a defined role in extracellular matrix remodeling, ion handling, inflammation, fibrosis, or intercellular signaling, it is not possible to establish a mechanistic connection to arrhythmogenesis from the supplied information alone.

### glycosaminoglycan binding (GO:0005539) 

Glycosaminoglycan binding refers to the selective interaction of proteins with sulfated or non-sulfated polysaccharides that are enriched on cell surfaces and within the extracellular matrix, especially heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, and related glycans carried by proteoglycans. These interactions are usually mediated by clusters of positively charged amino acid residues on the ligand and negatively charged sulfate and carboxyl groups on the glycosaminoglycan chain. In biological systems, glycosaminoglycan binding is not merely a passive adhesion event; it regulates ligand localization, retention, concentration, oligomerization, proteolytic processing, receptor accessibility, and downstream signaling. The publications provided indicate that this pathway may be particularly important for chemokine biology. Matrix metalloproteinase processing can increase glycosaminoglycan affinity of chemokines such as chemokine ligand sixteen, thereby altering inflammatory cell recruitment and tissue inflammatory tone (PubMed:22147696). Other studies show that chemokines can either require glycosaminoglycan engagement for endothelial presentation and gradient formation or competitively inhibit this process, as reported for chemokine ligand eighteen, chemokine ligand nine-derived peptides, chemokine ligand seven, and chemokine ligand seven structural studies with heparin (PubMed:23951310, PubMed:26183778, PubMed:24727473, PubMed:28245630). In addition, glycosaminoglycan engagement can itself trigger endothelial signaling and cytoskeletal remodeling, as illustrated for chemokine ligand eight acting through endothelial proteoglycans such as syndecan four (PubMed:29207576). Beyond inflammation, glycosaminoglycan binding is also mechanistically linked to coagulation biology because heparin binds antithrombin and strongly modulates factor tena inhibition, highlighting how glycosaminoglycan recognition may influence thrombosis-related cardiovascular disease states (PubMed:22453684). Taken together, glycosaminoglycan binding appears to function as a matrix and cell-surface organizing principle that integrates inflammatory signaling, endothelial activation, extracellular ligand distribution, and thromboregulatory processes, all of which may be relevant to cardiac electrical stability and structural remodeling.

Building on this functional overview, the available literature supports an indirect but biologically credible connection between glycosaminoglycan binding and arrhythmia through inflammatory remodeling, endothelial activation, and thrombosis-associated cardiovascular pathology rather than through a primary ion-channel mechanism. Several studies indicate that glycosaminoglycan binding governs chemokine immobilization on endothelial surfaces, the formation of chemotactic gradients, and leukocyte recruitment, all of which are central to chronic inflammation. Matrix metalloproteinase-mediated processing can enhance glycosaminoglycan binding of chemokines and increase monocyte-attracting activity, thereby favoring sustained inflammatory cell infiltration (PubMed:22147696). Chemokine ligand eighteen and a chemokine ligand nine-derived peptide can inhibit leukocyte recruitment by displacing chemokines from glycosaminoglycans, suggesting that glycosaminoglycan occupancy may be a decisive checkpoint for inflammatory trafficking (PubMed:23951310, PubMed:26183778). Chemokine ligand seven studies further indicate that glycosaminoglycan density regulates chemokine accumulation on cell surfaces, while structural work on chemokine ligand seven shows that glycosaminoglycan engagement can compete with receptor-binding interfaces and thereby reshape signaling outputs (PubMed:24727473, PubMed:28245630). Importantly, endothelial glycosaminoglycan engagement is not only a scaffold for chemokine presentation but also a signaling event that alters cytoskeletal organization and endothelial behavior, as shown for chemokine ligand eight in endothelial cells (PubMed:29207576). In the context of arrhythmia, these mechanisms may be relevant because atrial and ventricular arrhythmias commonly arise in hearts affected by inflammation-driven structural remodeling, extracellular matrix alteration, and endothelial dysfunction, which together promote conduction heterogeneity and reentry. This interpretation is further supported by the cardiovascular relevance of glycosaminoglycan-dependent heparin binding in antithrombin activation and the established importance of thrombosis in atrial fibrillation and cardioembolic disease (PubMed:22453684). Although the cited publications do not directly demonstrate that glycosaminoglycan binding alters cardiac excitability, they collectively suggest that this pathway may influence arrhythmia susceptibility by regulating inflammatory recruitment, matrix-associated signaling, vascular responses, and prothrombotic states that are closely linked to the arrhythmogenic substrate.[PubMed:22147696](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22147696) [PubMed:23951310](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23951310) [PubMed:26183778](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26183778) [PubMed:24727473](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24727473) [PubMed:28245630](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28245630) [PubMed:29207576](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29207576) [PubMed:22453684](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22453684) 

Consistent with this mechanistic framework, there were 30 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of glycosaminoglycan binding, a molecular function centered on the selective interaction of proteins with sulfated or non-sulfated polysaccharides located on cell surfaces and within the extracellular matrix. This enrichment is biologically notable because glycosaminoglycan binding regulates ligand retention, spatial concentration, oligomerization, proteolytic processing, receptor accessibility, and downstream signaling, thereby connecting extracellular matrix organization with inflammatory regulation, endothelial activation, and thromboregulatory control. The pathway description further indicates that these interactions depend on electrostatic complementarity between positively charged amino acid clusters and negatively charged sulfate and carboxyl groups, providing a clear physicochemical basis for the observed functional enrichment. In the context of arrhythmia, this may be particularly relevant because inflammatory signaling, endothelial perturbation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and coagulation-related vascular responses are all processes that can influence cardiac electrical stability and structural remodeling. The cited literature supports this interpretation with multiple mechanistic examples, including matrix metalloproteinase-dependent enhancement of glycosaminoglycan affinity for chemokine ligand sixteen that alters inflammatory cell recruitment (PubMed:22147696), glycosaminoglycan-dependent endothelial presentation and competitive modulation of chemokine gradients involving chemokine ligand eighteen, chemokine ligand nine-derived peptides, chemokine ligand seven, and heparin-binding structural determinants (PubMed:23951310, PubMed:26183778, PubMed:24727473, PubMed:28245630), endothelial signaling and cytoskeletal remodeling triggered by chemokine ligand eight through proteoglycans such as syndecan four (PubMed:29207576), and heparin-mediated modulation of antithrombin and factor tena inhibition in coagulation biology (PubMed:22453684). Collectively, these data support the interpretation that the 30 enriched proteins converge on a function that is quantitatively substantial and mechanistically positioned at the interface of inflammation, vascular biology, extracellular matrix dynamics, and cardiovascular pathophysiology relevant to arrhythmia.

To complement this pathway-level interpretation, the figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 30 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for interactive inspection: [Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=7228EF6114A784BC).

![PPI Network](imgs/f95e9d23-18de-40af-b4a8-bc4e1154f235.png)

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified several significant proteins. We introduce them in detail below.

Among the listed proteins, TGFBR2 is one of the most compelling candidates for relevance to arrhythmia because transforming growth factor beta signaling is a central driver of cardiac remodeling, particularly fibrosis. Atrial and ventricular arrhythmias commonly emerge in structurally remodeled myocardium, where excess extracellular matrix deposition disrupts electrical continuity, slows conduction, and promotes re-entry. The described functions of TGFBR2 in wound healing, extracellular matrix production, mesenchymal proliferation and differentiation, and non-canonical apoptotic signaling are highly consistent with mechanisms that generate an arrhythmogenic substrate. In addition, transforming growth factor beta-dependent epithelial and mesenchymal transition-like programs and fibroblast activation are well-recognized contributors to pathological remodeling after cardiac stress or injury. Thus, even though the annotation is not heart-specific, the biology of TGFBR2 appears to align closely with established mechanisms underlying fibrosis-associated atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmogenesis.[PubMed:33914044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33914044) 

Following this fibrosis-centered example, several additional proteins point toward vascular and endothelial mechanisms that may also shape arrhythmia susceptibility.

VEGFA stands out because myocardial perfusion, endothelial integrity, and microvascular signaling are tightly linked to arrhythmia susceptibility. The annotated roles of VEGFA in vascular development, endothelial survival, nitric oxide signaling, and cytoskeletal reorganization suggest several routes by which it may influence cardiac electrophysiology. Impaired or maladaptive VEGFA signaling can contribute to ischemia, altered vascular permeability, inflammatory remodeling, and endothelial dysfunction, all of which may destabilize cardiac conduction and repolarization. Its ability to activate AKT, MAPK, FAK, SRC, and NOS pathways is particularly relevant, as these pathways modulate cardiomyocyte survival, tissue remodeling, and vascular-cardiac coupling. In arrhythmia pathogenesis, especially in ischemic or heart failure settings, abnormal angiogenic signaling may therefore help shape both the structural substrate and the stress environment that promotes atrial or ventricular rhythm disturbances.
