In a related manner, extracellular matrix regulators within the enriched set may contribute to the structural substrate that supports conduction heterogeneity.

THBS2 is relevant to arrhythmia primarily through its likely contribution to extracellular matrix remodeling and antiangiogenic signaling. Cell-matrix interactions are critical determinants of myocardial architecture, and altered matrix composition is a hallmark of fibrotic remodeling in arrhythmogenic hearts. The antiangiogenic property of THBS2 may additionally influence myocardial oxygen delivery and reparative responses after injury, potentially favoring scar formation and conduction heterogeneity. Such changes can create the substrate for slowed conduction and re-entry. Although the provided annotation is concise, the combination of matrix adhesion and angiogenesis regulation makes THBS2 biologically plausible as a modifier of structural remodeling processes that predispose to arrhythmia.

Extending this matrix-centered theme, proteoglycan-associated components may also be relevant because they influence tissue organization and cell-matrix communication.

VCAN is notable because extracellular matrix proteoglycans are major determinants of tissue mechanics and electrical continuity in the heart. By linking cells to the extracellular matrix and influencing cell motility, growth, and differentiation, VCAN may contribute to the remodeling environment that supports arrhythmia. Its binding to hyaluronic acid further suggests a role in matrix organization and hydration, both of which can affect fibroblast behavior and tissue structure. In the context of atrial fibrillation or post-injury ventricular arrhythmia, matrix expansion and altered cell-matrix coupling are central mechanisms that disrupt impulse propagation. Therefore, VCAN is relevant as a potential contributor to the structural substrate underlying conduction heterogeneity and re-entrant arrhythmias.

A similar line of reasoning applies to fibrillar matrix components that may alter myocardial stiffness and intercellular electrical coupling.

COL5A1 is of interest because collagen composition is a key determinant of myocardial stiffness and conduction properties. Although type one and type three collagens are most often emphasized in cardiac fibrosis, type five collagen contributes to fibrillar collagen organization and therefore may influence the architecture of the extracellular matrix. In arrhythmia, especially atrial fibrillation, fibrotic remodeling leads to electrical uncoupling between cardiomyocyte bundles and promotes anisotropic conduction. The interaction of COL5A1 with heparan sulfate and thrombospondin also suggests broader participation in matrix signaling networks. Thus, COL5A1 may be relevant as a structural regulator of fibrotic substrate formation rather than a direct electrophysiologic effector.

Alongside fibrillar collagens, basement membrane-associated proteins may also be important because they help preserve myocardial microarchitecture.

PRELP is potentially relevant to arrhythmia through its role in matrix anchoring and tissue structural integrity. Basement membrane organization influences cellular alignment, mechanical stability, and signaling between parenchymal cells and stromal compartments. In the heart, disruption of these matrix relationships can facilitate maladaptive remodeling and alter conduction pathways. While the annotation is limited, proteins that organize basement membrane-connective tissue interfaces can be important in preserving normal myocardial microarchitecture. Consequently, PRELP may be indirectly linked to arrhythmia susceptibility by affecting the extracellular scaffold on which normal impulse propagation depends.

Beyond structural matrix proteins, several enriched factors may connect glycosaminoglycan binding to inflammation, repair, and endothelial activation after injury.

MDK is one of the most biologically interesting proteins in relation to arrhythmia because it integrates several processes known to promote arrhythmogenic remodeling: inflammation, angiogenesis, cell survival, tissue repair, endothelial activation, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition-like signaling. The annotation specifically notes roles in inflammatory cell recruitment, tissue regeneration after injury, vascular endothelial proliferation, VEGFA induction, nitric oxide synthase activation, and MAPK and AKT signaling. These functions are highly relevant to post-injury and heart failure-associated arrhythmias, where inflammation and reparative fibrosis reshape the myocardial substrate. Its capacity to regulate leukocyte recruitment and endothelial behavior suggests that MDK may influence both acute injury responses and chronic remodeling. Moreover, its role in promoting cell migration and epithelial and mesenchymal transition-related programs could contribute to fibrogenic remodeling, thereby increasing conduction heterogeneity and arrhythmia risk.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) 

Closely related growth factor-like signaling may also be represented by PTN, which appears to intersect with vascular support and tissue repair.

PTN is relevant to arrhythmia because it combines growth factor signaling, endothelial migration, cell survival, and regenerative biology, all of which intersect with cardiac remodeling. The annotation highlights activation of phosphoinositide three-kinase and protein kinase B pathways and mitogen-activated protein kinase pathways, endothelial migration via integrin complexes, and roles in hematopoietic regeneration and tissue growth. These processes can influence myocardial repair, vascular support, and stromal-cardiomyocyte interactions after injury. Although PTN is better characterized in neural and developmental contexts, its pro-survival and migratory signaling suggests a plausible role in remodeling environments that predispose to arrhythmia. In particular, factors that alter endothelial behavior and matrix-cell signaling can indirectly modulate fibrosis, ischemic vulnerability, and conduction stability.[PubMed:11414790](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11414790) [PubMed:15121180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15121180) [PubMed:16619002](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16619002) [PubMed:17121547](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17121547) [PubMed:19442624](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19442624) [PubMed:21791434](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21791434) [PubMed:25000129](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25000129) [PubMed:27445335](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27445335) [PubMed:28657144](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28657144) [PubMed:30497772](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30497772) 

Another protein with a potentially important injury-response profile is FSTL1, which may be especially relevant in the stressed myocardium.

FSTL1 is particularly notable for arrhythmia-related biology because the annotation directly includes promotion of cardiac myocyte survival as well as endothelial survival, migration, and angiogenic differentiation in an AKT-dependent manner. These functions are highly relevant in the injured or failing heart, where myocyte loss, vascular insufficiency, and inflammatory remodeling contribute to electrical instability. A molecule that supports cardiomyocyte viability and vascular repair could modify the extent of scar formation and the persistence of arrhythmogenic substrate. In addition, its links to immune regulation and bone morphogenetic protein and toll-like receptor four-associated signaling suggest broader roles in inflammatory and reparative responses, both of which are strongly implicated in atrial and ventricular arrhythmias.[PubMed:19595790](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19595790) [PubMed:20054002](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20054002) [PubMed:21826198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21826198) 

In a similar reparative and angiogenic context, fibroblast growth factor-associated modulation may also contribute to the remodeling environment.

FGFBP1 is relevant because fibroblast growth factor-axis signaling contributes to tissue repair, angiogenesis, and fibroblast-endothelial communication, all of which can influence arrhythmogenic remodeling. The annotation emphasizes mitogenic activity, angiogenesis, integrin binding, and extracellular signal-regulated kinase one and two activation, suggesting that FGFBP1 may amplify growth factor responses in remodeling tissues. In the heart, excessive or imbalanced proliferative and angiogenic signaling can alter stromal composition and vascular support, thereby affecting conduction properties indirectly. While FGFBP1 is not a classic arrhythmia gene, its ability to coordinate fibroblast growth factor receptor and integrin signaling makes it a plausible modifier of the structural and vascular milieu associated with arrhythmia susceptibility.[PubMed:8663044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8663044) [PubMed:1721615](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1721615) [PubMed:3732516](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3732516) [PubMed:3964259](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3964259) [PubMed:23469107](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23469107) [PubMed:28302677](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28302677) [PubMed:29501879](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29501879) 

Beyond these growth factor-associated proteins, pathway modulators of fibrosis and vascular remodeling may also warrant attention.

SFRP1 deserves attention because Wnt and beta-catenin signaling is a major regulator of fibrosis, repair, and cellular differentiation in the cardiovascular system. By antagonizing Wnt signaling and lowering beta-catenin levels, SFRP1 could influence fibroblast activation, vascular remodeling, and tissue regeneration after injury. These processes are highly pertinent to arrhythmia, particularly atrial fibrillation, where dysregulated profibrotic signaling contributes to substrate formation. The annotation also notes vascular cell cycle effects and angiogenic responses, further supporting a role in remodeling rather than direct ion-channel regulation. Thus, SFRP1 may be important as a pathway-level modulator of structural and vascular changes that affect cardiac rhythm stability.

Another extracellular matrix-associated candidate is SMOC2, which may link matrix assembly to endothelial behavior.

SMOC2 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because it links extracellular matrix assembly with endothelial activation. Matrix assembly and cell adhesion shape tissue architecture, while angiogenesis and endothelial migration influence perfusion and repair. In arrhythmogenic remodeling, especially after ischemic or inflammatory injury, aberrant matrix deposition and altered vascular responses create heterogeneous conduction zones. Therefore, although SMOC2 is not directly tied to electrophysiology in the annotation, its combined effects on matrix organization and angiogenesis make it a plausible contributor to the structural substrate that supports arrhythmia.

A somewhat more tentative connection may be considered for adhesion-related receptors that influence mechanotransduction and tissue organization.

ADGRG1 is a more speculative but still interesting candidate because cell adhesion receptors and RhoA-associated signaling can influence tissue architecture, mechanotransduction, and remodeling. Although the provided annotation emphasizes neural development, hematopoietic stem cell maintenance, and tumorigenesis, the core biology of cell-matrix adhesion and RhoA pathway activation is relevant to fibroblast behavior and structural remodeling in the heart. Since arrhythmias often arise from altered tissue coupling and matrix organization, proteins that regulate adhesion signaling may contribute indirectly to disease susceptibility. However, compared with TGFBR2, VEGFA, MDK, or FSTL1, the connection of ADGRG1 to arrhythmia appears less direct based on the current annotation.[PubMed:21768377](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21768377) [PubMed:23478665](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23478665) [PubMed:20981830](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20981830) 

Similarly, matrix-sensing proteins associated with hyaluronate-rich environments may reflect inflammatory or injury-related remodeling states.

LAYN may be relevant to arrhythmia because hyaluronate-rich extracellular matrices are characteristic of tissue injury, inflammation, and remodeling. Receptors for hyaluronate can regulate cell adhesion, migration, and inflammatory cell behavior, all of which may influence the development of fibrotic or edematous myocardial substrate. Although the annotation is minimal, this matrix-sensing role suggests a plausible indirect connection to arrhythmia through extracellular matrix remodeling and inflammatory responses.

Finally, fibrinolysis-related extracellular proteins may have a more limited but still potentially relevant role in matrix turnover and scar organization.

CLEC3B is of possible interest because plasminogen-related biology intersects with extracellular matrix turnover and fibrinolytic balance. Matrix degradation and remodeling are important determinants of scar organization and conduction heterogeneity in arrhythmogenic heart disease. However, the current annotation provides only limited support for a direct or strong arrhythmia link. Its relevance is therefore likely secondary and substantially weaker than that of proteins involved in transforming growth factor beta signaling, angiogenesis, or inflammatory remodeling.

### Viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor (KEGG:04061) 

The pathway entitled viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor describes a host pathogen interface in which viral proteins directly or indirectly alter cytokine production, cytokine receptor signaling, and downstream inflammatory responses. Cytokines are soluble immune mediators that regulate leukocyte recruitment, endothelial activation, vascular permeability, tissue repair, and cell survival, whereas cytokine receptors transmit these signals into intracellular programs involving mitogen activated protein kinase signaling, nuclear factor kappa B activation, and other stress responsive pathways. In the setting of viral infection, viral structural proteins, nonstructural proteins, or virus induced host factors can amplify proinflammatory cytokine release, sensitize target tissues to cytokine signaling, or disrupt normal negative feedback regulation of these pathways. The publications provided emphasize that severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus two is strongly linked to excessive inflammatory cytokine production, particularly interleukin six, tumor necrosis factor alpha, and other inflammatory mediators, together with myocardial injury, endothelial dysfunction, thrombosis, and electrical instability of the heart. In parallel, evidence from Kaposi sarcoma associated herpesvirus shows that viral regulation of host signaling suppressors such as dual specificity phosphatase one can sustain mitogen activated protein kinase activity and promote cytokine associated pathogenic programs, illustrating a broader principle by which viruses potentiate cytokine receptor signaling and tissue injury. Taken together, this pathway appears biologically relevant to arrhythmia because abnormal viral modulation of cytokine and cytokine receptor networks may create a systemic and myocardial inflammatory environment that alters cardiomyocyte electrophysiology, promotes structural injury, and destabilizes cardiac rhythm.

Against this biological background, the relationship between this pathway and arrhythmia can be understood more clearly through the capacity of viral infection to provoke maladaptive cytokine and cytokine receptor signaling that secondarily injures the myocardium and perturbs cardiac electrical homeostasis. The coronavirus disease nineteen literature consistently indicates that infection is accompanied by marked elevation of inflammatory mediators, especially interleukin six and tumor necrosis factor alpha, and that these inflammatory signals correlate with myocardial injury biomarkers, myocarditis, ventricular dysfunction, and clinically observed arrhythmias. One review describes overproduction of inflammatory cytokines as a central feature of severe infection and explicitly links this inflammatory hyperactivity with cardiac injury and increased occurrence of arrhythmias, myocarditis, and cardiomyopathy, suggesting that cytokine driven myocardial inflammation may represent an important mechanistic bridge between viral infection and rhythm disturbance (PubMed:32719447). A second review similarly notes increased concentrations of interleukin two, interleukin six, ferritin, and C reactive protein in affected patients and identifies cytokine release, especially interleukin six mediated injury, as a plausible cause of myocardial inflammation, necrosis, ventricular dysfunction, and arrhythmia (PubMed:34258904). Additional work on severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus two host receptor interactions expands this concept by showing that viral engagement of angiotensin converting enzyme two and other host receptors contributes to hypertension, myocardial injury, arrhythmia, and coagulation abnormalities, thereby indicating that viral receptor biology and cytokine network activation may cooperate to produce an arrhythmogenic substrate (PubMed:36088078). Clinical cardiovascular reviews further reinforce that coronavirus disease nineteen is associated with acute myocardial injury, myocarditis, stress related cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, and cardiac arrest, and they highlight the need for rhythm monitoring in infected patients because inflammatory and myocardial complications are frequent (PubMed:32354800). Although not focused on arrhythmia directly, the Kaposi sarcoma associated herpesvirus study is mechanistically informative because it demonstrates that a virus can suppress dual specificity phosphatase one, thereby sustaining mitogen activated protein kinase signaling and cytokine associated pathogenic programs; this supports the broader inference that viral enhancement of cytokine receptor signaling can intensify tissue inflammation and potentially favor electrical instability when such processes occur in the heart (PubMed:23097457). Taken together, the pathway is related to arrhythmia because viral manipulation of cytokine and cytokine receptor signaling promotes systemic inflammation, myocardial inflammation, endothelial and microvascular injury, and structural cardiac damage, all of which are well established substrates for abnormal impulse generation and conduction.[PubMed:32719447](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32719447) [PubMed:34258904](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34258904) [PubMed:36088078](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36088078) [PubMed:32354800](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32354800) [PubMed:23097457](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23097457) 

Building on this literature based rationale, the enrichment results provide a quantitative indication that this pathway may capture a meaningful component of the arrhythmia associated protein landscape. There were 27 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway entitled viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor, indicating that this host pathogen inflammatory signaling axis captures a substantial functional module within the analyzed protein set. This enrichment is biologically notable because the pathway connects viral perturbation of cytokine production and cytokine receptor signaling with downstream inflammatory and stress responsive programs that are highly relevant to arrhythmia pathogenesis, including myocardial injury, endothelial dysfunction, thrombosis, altered vascular permeability, and electrical instability of the heart. In particular, the pathway description highlights excessive inflammatory cytokine production, especially interleukin six and tumor necrosis factor alpha, together with sustained signaling through mitogen activated protein kinase and nuclear factor kappa B related mechanisms, providing a data supported framework through which viral inflammatory signaling may alter cardiomyocyte electrophysiology, impair tissue integrity, and destabilize cardiac rhythm in arrhythmia.

To further contextualize these 27 proteins, the interaction network offers an additional systems level view of how these factors may be functionally connected within inflammatory signaling processes relevant to cardiac instability. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 27 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for interactive network exploration: [https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=E7C1262862C9D111](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=E7C1262862C9D111).

![PPI Network](imgs/ec315c13-02fd-4a6b-8a8a-870a0c891b51.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=E7C1262862C9D111)

With this network context in place, the function enrichment analysis next highlights several proteins that may contribute to the observed pathway level signal and therefore merit individual consideration. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following. CCL14 stands out because its annotated activity is tightly linked to inflammatory chemokine handling, a process with clear mechanistic relevance to arrhythmia, particularly atrial fibrillation and inflammation-associated electrical remodeling. Although this protein is not a canonical ion-channel regulator, its ability to control the local and systemic availability of chemokines such as CCL2, CCL5, and CXCL8 is potentially important in the cardiac setting, where inflammatory cell recruitment contributes to myocardial injury, fibrosis, and conduction heterogeneity. These structural and inflammatory changes are well-recognized substrates for arrhythmogenesis. The endothelial transcytosis function is especially notable, because leukocyte adhesion and transmigration across the cardiac microvasculature can amplify local inflammatory responses, while the erythrocyte-associated chemokine sink function may modulate circulating inflammatory burden. Thus, the most meaningful connection to arrhythmia is likely indirect but biologically plausible: dysregulation of inflammatory chemokine sequestration and presentation could influence myocardial inflammation, immune-cell infiltration, and fibrotic remodeling, all of which can promote abnormal impulse generation and re-entry. However, based on the provided annotation alone, the evidence supports CCL14 primarily as a modulator of inflammatory tone rather than as a direct arrhythmia effector.

### Lung fibrosis (WP:WP3624) 

Lung fibrosis is a chronic pathological process characterized by excessive deposition of extracellular matrix, expansion and activation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, distortion of normal alveolar architecture, progressive stiffening of the lung, and impairment of gas exchange. It commonly develops in response to persistent epithelial injury, dysregulated wound healing, inflammatory signaling, macrophage activation, oxidative stress, and profibrotic mediators such as transforming growth factor beta. Recent mechanistic work has further suggested that alveolar macrophage intrinsic signaling can directly regulate fibrotic progression; for example, loss of pleckstrin homology domain and leucine rich repeat protein phosphatase one enhances a Kruppel like factor four centered profibrotic transcriptional program and worsens pulmonary fibrosis, indicating that immune epigenetic control may be integral to this pathway (PubMed:40085643). Although lung fibrosis is anatomically centered in the lung, its biological consequences extend beyond the respiratory system. Progressive pulmonary fibrosis can increase pulmonary vascular resistance, promote pulmonary hypertension, cause chronic hypoxemia, trigger systemic inflammation and oxidative stress, and ultimately impose pressure overload on the right ventricle and right atrium. Through these cardiopulmonary interactions, lung fibrosis may contribute to structural and electrical remodeling of the heart, including chamber dilation, myocardial inflammation, altered connexin distribution, ion channel remodeling, and myocardial fibrosis. Thus, the lung fibrosis pathway may be viewed not only as a pulmonary remodeling program but also as a potential driver of secondary cardiac remodeling that could create a substrate for both atrial and ventricular arrhythmias.  

Building on this pathophysiological framework, the publications collectively suggest that the relationship between lung fibrosis and arrhythmia is mediated primarily through cardiopulmonary remodeling, fibrosis associated electrical instability, and disease states in which pulmonary fibrotic injury coexists with cardiac structural abnormalities. Clinically, patients undergoing lung transplantation showed a high burden of postoperative atrial arrhythmia, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis was more frequent among affected individuals, while elevated right atrial pressure independently predicted atrial arrhythmia and this complication was associated with worse long term survival, supporting the concept that fibrotic lung disease may contribute to arrhythmogenic right sided loading conditions and atrial remodeling (PubMed:31752476). Experimental and review studies of right heart disease further support this connection by showing that pulmonary vascular and lung driven pressure overload can produce right ventricular and right atrial hypertrophy, dilation, inflammation, fibrosis, and vulnerability to both atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmias; importantly, pulmonary artery banding reproduced this phenotype without direct toxic lung injury, suggesting that cardiopulmonary mechanical stress alone may generate an arrhythmogenic substrate (PubMed:39283087, PubMed:41001267). In pulmonary arterial hypertension, which often develops in the setting of chronic pulmonary remodeling, myocardial fibrosis appears to emerge as a central mechanism linking pressure overload to conduction abnormalities, connexin forty three dysregulation, ion channel remodeling, and malignant arrhythmia susceptibility, and several interventions that reduce fibrosis also reduce ventricular arrhythmias in preclinical models (PubMed:38542257, PubMed:41371472, PubMed:40824146). More broadly, the arrhythmia literature consistently identifies fibrosis as a key substrate for abnormal impulse conduction and re entry: in persistent atrial fibrillation, left atrial fibrosis detected by magnetic resonance imaging is strongly implicated in pathophysiology and recurrence risk even though fibrosis targeted ablation did not improve outcomes and increased adverse events, indicating that fibrosis is biologically important but not easily neutralized procedurally (PubMed:35727277); in systemic sclerosis, diffuse myocardial fibrosis measured by extracellular volume was associated with clinically significant arrhythmias (PubMed:30690570); and in non ischemic cardiomyopathy, fibrosis heterogeneity strongly predicted life threatening arrhythmia beyond left ventricular ejection fraction alone (PubMed:40932094, PubMed:36752459). Mechanistic modeling also shows that patchy fibrosis promotes focal excitation, wave break, and maintenance of atrial fibrillation by altering electrotonic load and conduction behavior (PubMed:38372694). Taken together, these studies support a coherent model in which lung fibrosis may promote pulmonary vascular and hemodynamic stress, systemic inflammation, and right heart remodeling, while fibrosis as a biological process may directly create the structural and electrophysiological substrate necessary for arrhythmia initiation and maintenance.[PubMed:40085643](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40085643) [PubMed:31752476](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31752476) [PubMed:39283087](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39283087) [PubMed:41001267](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41001267) [PubMed:38542257](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38542257) [PubMed:41371472](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41371472) [PubMed:40824146](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40824146) [PubMed:35727277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35727277) [PubMed:30690570](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30690570) [PubMed:40932094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40932094) [PubMed:36752459](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36752459) [PubMed:38372694](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38372694) 

Consistent with this literature context, there were 15 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing lung fibrosis as a chronic pathological process characterized by excessive extracellular matrix deposition, fibroblast and myofibroblast expansion, distortion of alveolar structure, progressive tissue stiffening, impaired gas exchange, persistent epithelial injury, dysregulated wound healing, inflammatory signaling, macrophage activation, oxidative stress, and transforming growth factor beta driven profibrotic remodeling, with additional evidence that loss of pleckstrin homology domain and leucine rich repeat protein phosphatase one in alveolar macrophages amplifies a Kruppel like factor four centered profibrotic transcriptional program and worsens pulmonary fibrosis (PubMed:40085643). This enrichment supports a quantitatively defined interpretation in which a set of 15 proteins links arrhythmia to a cardiopulmonary remodeling axis, where progressive pulmonary fibrosis can elevate pulmonary vascular resistance, increase pulmonary hypertension burden, promote chronic hypoxemia, intensify systemic inflammation and oxidative stress, and thereby drive right ventricular and right atrial pressure overload, chamber remodeling, myocardial fibrosis, altered connexin distribution, ion channel remodeling, and ultimately both atrial and ventricular electrical instability relevant to arrhythmia pathogenesis.

To complement this enrichment result, the figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 15 proteins, together with the corresponding STRING webpage link for direct inspection of the interaction map and supporting evidence.

![PPI Network](imgs/f1c6bfb9-abf6-4875-994d-ca38a34df11d.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=0A8AE38E365BEBC7)

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
With this network level context in place, it is useful to consider the individual proteins in order of their likely relevance to arrhythmia within the broader lung fibrosis framework.

Among the proteins listed, ELN has the most plausible and substantial connection to arrhythmia. Although elastin is not a canonical ion-channel or sarcomeric arrhythmia gene, its central role in vascular wall architecture and aortic integrity makes it highly relevant to cardiovascular disease states that can secondarily promote arrhythmogenesis. ELN supports terminal differentiation and maturation of vascular smooth muscle cells and preserves the biomechanical properties of the aortic wall, while also coordinating extracellular matrix cross-linking through LOX and collagen-elastin assembly (PubMed:16478991, PubMed:19855011, PubMed:20019329, PubMed:26486174, PubMed:26711913, PubMed:28508064, PubMed:26178373, PubMed:26220971, PubMed:26690653, PubMed:17324935). Disturbance of these processes can contribute to arterial stiffness, abnormal vascular remodeling, and impaired hemodynamic buffering. These vascular abnormalities are clinically relevant because chronic pressure overload, increased afterload, and maladaptive remodeling can promote atrial and ventricular structural changes that create a substrate for arrhythmia, particularly atrial fibrillation and other rhythm disorders associated with cardiovascular remodeling. In addition, ELN-mediated effects on smooth muscle cell proliferation through angiotensin signaling suggest a link to neurohormonal pathways that are themselves strongly implicated in cardiac remodeling and arrhythmia susceptibility (PubMed:23636094). Thus, ELN stands out as the protein with the strongest indirect but biologically meaningful relationship to arrhythmia through vascular extracellular matrix integrity, hemodynamic stress, and remodeling-associated electrophysiologic vulnerability.[PubMed:16478991](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16478991) [PubMed:19855011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19855011) [PubMed:20019329](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019329) [PubMed:26486174](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26486174) [PubMed:26711913](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26711913) [PubMed:28508064](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28508064) [PubMed:26178373](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26178373) [PubMed:26220971](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26220971) [PubMed:26690653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26690653) [PubMed:17324935](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17324935) [PubMed:23636094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23636094) 

In contrast to ELN, the remaining proteins appear to have more indirect or context dependent relationships with arrhythmia, and this distinction helps organize the interpretation of the enriched set.

CALCA is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because calcium homeostasis is fundamental to cardiac electrophysiology, excitation-contraction coupling, and impulse propagation. Although the description provided here is limited to katacalcin as a plasma calcium-lowering peptide and does not directly describe myocardial actions, systemic perturbation of calcium balance can influence cardiac action potential dynamics, refractoriness, and triggered activity. In principle, peptides that alter calcium handling may affect arrhythmia susceptibility indirectly by modifying extracellular calcium availability, which is a key determinant of membrane stability and conduction behavior. However, compared with ELN, the arrhythmia connection for CALCA is less direct and less specifically supported by the functional annotation provided. Therefore, CALCA should be regarded as a secondary candidate of interest whose relevance derives from the broader importance of calcium regulation in arrhythmogenesis rather than from a clearly established structural or electrophysiologic mechanism in the heart.

A related but distinct line of reasoning applies to inflammatory and stress response pathways, which may influence arrhythmia susceptibility through myocardial remodeling rather than through direct electrophysiological function alone.

The function attributed here to IL12B suggests potential relevance to arrhythmia through inflammation, oxidative stress, and proteostasis, all of which are recognized contributors to electrical and structural remodeling in the heart. The described roles in modulating type I interferon responses, regulating autophagic degradation of signaling intermediates, and activating the KEAP1-NRF2 antioxidant pathway indicate involvement in cellular stress adaptation (PubMed:31916398, PubMed:34374750). These processes are mechanistically relevant because oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling can alter ion channel expression, gap junction integrity, calcium handling, and fibrotic remodeling, thereby increasing arrhythmia susceptibility. Nevertheless, the annotation provided does not establish a direct cardiac-specific role, and the protein description appears functionally closer to a selective autophagy adaptor than to the canonical immunologic role usually associated with IL12B. Accordingly, while this entry may point to biologically meaningful pathways linked to arrhythmogenesis, the connection remains indirect and should be interpreted cautiously.[PubMed:31916398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31916398) [PubMed:34374750](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34374750) 

Finally, the weakest candidate in this set appears to be a protein whose relevance is largely mediated through pulmonary physiology rather than through direct cardiac mechanisms.

SFTPA2 has the weakest apparent connection to arrhythmia among the listed proteins. Its primary function is pulmonary, where it contributes to surfactant biology and normal respiratory mechanics. A possible indirect relationship to arrhythmia could arise in the context of chronic lung dysfunction, hypoxemia, or pulmonary disease, all of which can increase the risk of atrial arrhythmias through hypoxia, pulmonary vascular stress, and right heart remodeling. However, the function provided does not indicate a direct role in cardiac electrophysiology, myocardial structure, calcium handling, or vascular remodeling. Therefore, SFTPA2 is unlikely to be a primary arrhythmia-relevant protein in this set, except in a broad systemic sense whereby impaired lung function may secondarily influence cardiac rhythm.

### Pleural mesothelioma (WP:WP5087) 

Pleural mesothelioma is a malignant disease arising from mesothelial cells lining the pleural surface and is classically associated with chronic asbestos exposure, prolonged local inflammation, genomic instability, and progressive invasion of thoracic structures. Contemporary molecular studies indicate that pleural mesothelioma is not a single uniform entity, but rather a heterogeneous disease shaped by recurrent alterations in genes such as BRCA1 associated protein 1, neurofibromin 2, and cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 2A, together with major variation in immune response, epigenetic state, ploidy, and tumor cell morphology across patients and even across different anatomic regions within the same patient. Multiomic analyses further show that extracellular matrix remodeling, cell adhesion programs, immune microenvironment states, and methylation patterns contribute substantially to disease behavior and treatment response. Clinically, pleural mesothelioma is managed through combinations of surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and selected targeted or metabolic therapies, although prognosis remains poor and treatment-related morbidity is substantial. Because the tumor develops within the hemithorax and frequently extends to the pericardium, myocardium, mediastinum, and neighboring pleural surfaces, this disease has important cardiopulmonary consequences beyond cancer progression alone. Taken together, these features suggest that the pleural mesothelioma pathway is best understood as an integrated oncologic process involving thoracic tumor growth, local invasion, inflammatory and immune remodeling, and treatment-associated systemic stress, all of which can influence cardiac electrical stability.  

Against this broader disease framework, the relationship between pleural mesothelioma and arrhythmia appears to be supported less by a single canonical intracellular arrhythmogenic signaling cascade than by the anatomic, pathophysiologic, and therapeutic consequences of this thoracic malignancy. Direct evidence of cardiac involvement is particularly strong: in a clinicopathologic study, electrocardiographic abnormalities were present in most patients with diffuse malignant pleural mesothelioma, about sixty percent had arrhythmias, and autopsy demonstrated cardiac invasion in nearly three quarters of examined cases, with frequent pericardial and myocardial extension. These observations suggest that tumor spread to cardiac structures may directly disturb impulse generation and conduction and thereby promote atrial and ventricular rhythm disorders (PubMed:3779621). Clinical reports also indicate that fatal cardiac arrhythmia can occur in patients with pleural mesothelioma in advanced disease settings (PubMed:36924064). In parallel, arrhythmia emerges repeatedly as a treatment-associated complication in multimodality management. Major thoracic surgery for pleural mesothelioma, especially extrapleural pneumonectomy or pleurectomy decortication based strategies, has been associated with substantial perioperative cardiac morbidity, including atrial fibrillation and supraventricular arrhythmias in surgical series and reviews, consistent with the combined effects of pericardial manipulation, inflammation, autonomic stress, hypoxia, fluid shifts, and postoperative cardiopulmonary strain (PubMed:21388982, PubMed:22453539, PubMed:17410047). The randomized comparison of surgery plus chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone also documented a higher incidence of serious cardiac disorders in the surgical arm, further supporting the view that aggressive local treatment may increase arrhythmic risk in this population (PubMed:38740044). Systemic therapies may also contribute: treatment-emergent death from atrial fibrillation was reported with anetumab ravtansine, cardiac arrhythmia occurred in patients receiving pirarubicin, belinostat was associated with a possibly treatment-related death from cardiac arrhythmia, and immunotherapy with nivolumab plus ipilimumab included treatment-related death from heart failure. Collectively, these findings suggest that both cytotoxic and immune-based interventions can exacerbate cardiac electrical instability in susceptible patients (PubMed:35358455, PubMed:2386894, PubMed:19096314, PubMed:33485464). Overall, the available evidence indicates that pleural mesothelioma may be related to arrhythmia through three converging mechanisms: direct tumor invasion of the pericardium and myocardium, indirect cardiopulmonary stress caused by advanced intrathoracic disease, and cardiotoxic or surgically induced complications arising during treatment.[PubMed:3779621](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3779621) [PubMed:36924064](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36924064) [PubMed:21388982](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21388982) [PubMed:22453539](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22453539) [PubMed:17410047](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17410047) [PubMed:38740044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38740044) [PubMed:35358455](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35358455) [PubMed:2386894](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2386894) [PubMed:19096314](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19096314) [PubMed:33485464](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33485464) 

Building on this disease level context, there were 38 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing pleural mesothelioma as a malignant thoracic disease characterized by chronic asbestos exposure, sustained local inflammation, genomic instability, extracellular matrix remodeling, immune and epigenetic heterogeneity, and progressive invasion into adjacent cardiopulmonary structures. This enrichment profile is notable because the pathway context explicitly connects thoracic tumor expansion, pericardial and myocardial extension, mediastinal involvement, inflammatory remodeling, and treatment-associated systemic stress with disturbed cardiac electrical stability, thereby providing a biologically plausible framework linking 38 proteins to arrhythmia-related mechanisms within a complex thoracic disease setting. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 38 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct network exploration.  
![PPI Network](imgs/bf7eca19-85ff-4a53-b4e2-2d50505a0194.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=4F5D2CAFE2644B38)

With this network level overview in place, the function enrichment analysis highlighted several significant proteins that may warrant closer consideration. We will introduce them in detail in the following.

Among the listed proteins, vascular endothelial growth factor A stands out as one of the most plausibly relevant to arrhythmia because myocardial electrical stability is tightly coupled to coronary microvascular integrity, tissue oxygenation, endothelial signaling, and structural remodeling. Vascular endothelial growth factor A mediated angiogenesis and endothelial survival may be protective in ischemic or pressure overloaded myocardium by preserving perfusion, whereas dysregulated vascular endothelial growth factor A signaling can also contribute to vascular permeability, edema, and maladaptive remodeling. Its induction of nitric oxide synthase 2 and nitric oxide synthase 3, together with nitric oxide production, is particularly notable because nitric oxide influences vascular tone, myocardial oxygen delivery, calcium handling, and electrophysiological properties that can modulate arrhythmia susceptibility. In addition, vascular endothelial growth factor A driven activation of phosphoinositide 3 kinase and protein kinase B, mitogen activated protein kinase, SRC proto-oncogene non-receptor tyrosine kinase, and focal adhesion kinase pathways links it to survival signaling and cytoskeletal remodeling, processes relevant to post-injury scar formation and conduction heterogeneity. Therefore, vascular endothelial growth factor A appears mechanistically connected to arrhythmogenesis primarily through ischemia-related injury, endothelial dysfunction, and structural remodeling of the myocardium and vasculature.  

In a related but somewhat broader remodeling context, midkine is highly relevant to arrhythmia because it integrates several biological processes that are central to the formation of an arrhythmogenic substrate, including inflammation, angiogenesis, cell survival, and tissue repair after injury. The protein promotes recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages to sites of inflammation and modulates immune cell differentiation, suggesting a role in inflammatory cardiac remodeling, which is increasingly recognized as a driver of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. Importantly, midkine has been reported to regulate inflammatory cell recruitment after heart damage, promote cell survival through mitogen activated protein kinase and protein kinase B anti-apoptotic signaling, and stimulate angiogenesis, all of which are directly pertinent to post-infarction remodeling and scar border zone instability. Its ability to induce vascular endothelial growth factor A expression further strengthens its connection to vascular remodeling, while its effects on smooth muscle migration and epithelial to mesenchymal transition imply broader roles in structural remodeling and fibrosis-like processes. Collectively, midkine may contribute to arrhythmia not as a classical ion channel regulator, but rather as a potent mediator of the inflammatory, reparative, and vascular pathways that reshape cardiac tissue and alter conduction.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) 

Shifting from soluble signaling mediators to structural determinants, actin alpha 2 is of potential interest in arrhythmia because cytoskeletal integrity is essential for normal cardiovascular structure and function. Although the provided annotation is general, actin dependent contractile and cytoskeletal networks are fundamental to vascular smooth muscle behavior and tissue mechanics. In the context of arrhythmia, abnormalities affecting cytoskeletal architecture can contribute indirectly by promoting vascular disease, altered myocardial loading conditions, and structural remodeling, all of which may facilitate atrial or ventricular electrical instability. Actin alpha 2 is therefore less directly linked to electrophysiology than vascular endothelial growth factor A or midkine, but it remains relevant as a structural gene whose perturbation could influence arrhythmia susceptibility through remodeling of the cardiovascular system.  

A similar emphasis on remodeling applies to secreted frizzled related protein 1, which is noteworthy because Wnt and beta catenin signaling is strongly implicated in cardiac development, fibroblast activation, and myocardial remodeling, all of which influence arrhythmia risk. By antagonizing Wnt signaling and reducing beta catenin levels, secreted frizzled related protein 1 could affect the balance between adaptive repair and maladaptive fibrosis after cardiac injury. Its antiproliferative effects on vascular cells also suggest a role in vascular remodeling, which may secondarily alter myocardial perfusion and substrate formation. While the annotation does not explicitly mention the heart, Wnt pathway modulators are often relevant to arrhythmogenesis because they can shape the structural environment in which conduction occurs, particularly in atrial fibrosis or post-injury ventricular remodeling. Thus, secreted frizzled related protein 1 may be mechanistically connected to arrhythmia through regulation of remodeling pathways rather than through direct control of ion channels.  

Continuing this theme of structural substrate formation, collagen triple helix repeat containing 1 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because extracellular matrix remodeling and fibrosis are major determinants of abnormal impulse propagation. A factor that negatively regulates collagen matrix deposition could influence whether injured myocardium develops diffuse fibrosis, patchy interstitial scarring, or a more limited reparative response. Since fibrotic remodeling slows conduction, increases anisotropy, and promotes re-entry, proteins that modulate collagen accumulation are of particular interest in both atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. Although the functional annotation here is brief, collagen triple helix repeat containing 1 stands out as a plausible regulator of arrhythmogenic structural remodeling through its effects on matrix composition.  

By comparison, mitotic arrest deficient 1 like 1 has a less direct connection to arrhythmia than the vascular and remodeling associated proteins in this list, but it may still be relevant in proliferative cell populations involved in cardiac repair, inflammation, or fibrosis. Proper spindle checkpoint function preserves genomic stability, and defects in such pathways can alter the behavior of fibroblasts, vascular cells, or inflammatory cells participating in post-injury remodeling. Because arrhythmia often emerges from structural and cellular remodeling rather than solely from cardiomyocyte autonomous defects, regulators of cell cycle fidelity can have indirect importance. Nevertheless, based on the provided annotation, mitotic arrest deficient 1 like 1 should be considered a secondary candidate compared with proteins more directly linked to angiogenesis, inflammation, or extracellular matrix regulation.[PubMed:10700282](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10700282) [PubMed:11804586](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11804586) [PubMed:15024386](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15024386) [PubMed:29162720](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29162720) 

Finally, extending the discussion from structural and inflammatory remodeling to systemic metabolic influences, fatty acid binding protein 4 is relevant to arrhythmia primarily through metabolic and adipose related mechanisms. Disturbed lipid handling, adipose inflammation, and ectopic fat deposition are increasingly recognized contributors to atrial arrhythmogenesis, especially in obesity-associated atrial fibrillation. As a fatty acid and retinoic acid chaperone, fatty acid binding protein 4 may influence systemic metabolic status, adipocyte signaling, and lipotoxic or inflammatory pathways that secondarily affect the heart. Although the provided annotation does not directly connect fatty acid binding protein 4 to electrophysiology, its role in adipocyte biology makes it a plausible mediator of the metabolic substrate that predisposes to arrhythmia, particularly where epicardial adipose tissue and inflammatory crosstalk are involved.

### Neutrophil degranulation (REAC:R-HSA-6798695) 

Neutrophil degranulation is a tightly regulated effector program of innate immunity in which activated neutrophils mobilize and release the contents of intracellular granule subsets to the cell surface, extracellular space, or phagocytic compartments. These granules contain proteases, oxidant-generating enzymes, antimicrobial peptides, matrix-remodeling enzymes, adhesion-regulating molecules, and inflammatory mediators. Sequential release of secretory vesicles, tertiary granules, secondary granules, and primary granules alters neutrophil adhesion, migration, pathogen killing, and communication with surrounding tissues. Although this response is essential for host defense, excessive or misdirected degranulation can injure host tissue by promoting oxidative stress, extracellular matrix degradation, endothelial dysfunction, vascular leakage, and amplification of inflammatory signaling. Reviews and mechanistic studies have shown that major degranulation products such as myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinase eight, matrix metalloproteinase nine, neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin, cathelicidin, arginase, and azurocidin contribute to both tissue injury and tissue remodeling, particularly in ischemic heart disease and inflammatory injury settings. In the heart, neutrophil degranulation is increasingly recognized as a biologically important process after myocardial infarction and ischemia reperfusion, where it participates in necrotic tissue clearance but can also worsen myocardial damage, wall thinning, and adverse remodeling. This balance is further shaped by cross-talk with platelets and macrophages, because platelet serotonin can intensify neutrophil degranulation whereas macrophage-derived mediators can either restrain or amplify granule release. Thus, neutrophil degranulation should be understood as a dual-purpose inflammatory pathway whose pathological overactivation can transform a protective immune response into a driver of structural and electrophysiological cardiac disease.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature supports a meaningful, although still cautious, link between neutrophil degranulation and arrhythmia, especially atrial fibrillation, through convergent mechanisms involving inflammation, immune cell infiltration, oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodeling, and structural alteration of atrial tissue. Most directly, proteomic analysis of human left atrial tissue demonstrated that neutrophil degranulation is an over-represented biological process in atrial fibrillation and that its components are extensively shared with other dysregulated processes in the diseased atrium, including metabolic disturbance, cellular component disassembly, and ion homeostasis. This pattern suggests that the pathway may occupy a central position in the atrial disease network rather than representing an isolated inflammatory signal. The same study also showed increased presence of activated neutrophils and increased expression of neutrophil granule genes in atrial tissue from affected patients, supporting local activation of this pathway in the arrhythmic substrate (PubMed:33536523). Complementary transcriptomic and Mendelian randomization analyses further identified enrichment of neutrophil degranulation, specific granule formation, and tertiary granule pathways among genes associated with atrial fibrillation risk, together with immune infiltration signatures that included neutrophils, thereby reinforcing the concept that neutrophil-driven inflammatory programs are integrated into the molecular architecture of atrial fibrillation (PubMed:39055656). A separate systems-level analysis of atrial fibrillation also found enrichment of immune pathways including neutrophil degranulation in association with altered immune microenvironment and diagnostic gene signatures, again placing this pathway within the broader immunopathology of arrhythmia (PubMed:40329965). Mechanistically, evidence from cardiovascular injury models helps explain how neutrophil degranulation could contribute to arrhythmogenesis. In myocardial infarction, neutrophil granule products such as myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinase eight, matrix metalloproteinase nine, and neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin participate in early injury and later repair, but excessive release promotes extracellular matrix breakdown, inflammatory amplification, and adverse remodeling, all of which are established substrates for conduction heterogeneity and atrial or ventricular arrhythmia development (PubMed:35410418). Experimental work further showed that platelet serotonin aggravates myocardial ischemia reperfusion injury by inducing neutrophil degranulation, with increased myeloperoxidase release, hydrogen peroxide generation, and leukocyte adhesion, demonstrating a direct route by which thromboinflammation can intensify myocardial injury and thereby increase the probability of arrhythmogenic remodeling (PubMed:30586717). In addition, macrophage-derived signals after myocardial infarction can either suppress or augment neutrophil degranulation and thereby influence infarct wall thinning, indicating that the extent of granule release is functionally linked to structural remodeling of injured myocardium, a major determinant of electrical instability (PubMed:35230372). More broadly, reviews of hypoxic inflammation show that low-oxygen environments enhance secretion of destructive neutrophil granule contents, which is relevant because hypoxia, ischemia, and inflamed atrial tissue are common features in many arrhythmia-prone cardiac conditions. Such enhanced degranulation would be expected to intensify oxidative injury, fibroblast activation, and extracellular matrix turnover, thereby favoring the creation of a reentrant substrate (PubMed:32053993). Taken together, the publications suggest that neutrophil degranulation is related to arrhythmia not merely as a marker of inflammation, but also as a plausible mechanistic contributor to atrial and myocardial remodeling through protease release, oxidant production, immune amplification, and matrix disruption, with the strongest direct evidence currently available for atrial fibrillation.[PubMed:33536523](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33536523) [PubMed:39055656](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39055656) [PubMed:40329965](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40329965) [PubMed:35410418](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35410418) [PubMed:30586717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30586717) [PubMed:35230372](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35230372) [PubMed:32053993](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32053993) 

Consistent with this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment results also indicate a quantitatively substantial overlap between arrhythmia-associated proteins and this innate immune pathway. There were 48 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of neutrophil degranulation, indicating substantial convergence of arrhythmia-related molecular signals on an innate immune effector program that governs granule mobilization, extracellular protease release, oxidant generation, matrix remodeling, and inflammatory amplification. This protein count of 48 supports the interpretation that neutrophil-driven inflammatory injury is not a marginal feature but a quantitatively prominent component of the enriched functional landscape in arrhythmia. Given that neutrophil degranulation regulates the release of myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinase eight, matrix metalloproteinase nine, neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin, cathelicidin, arginase, and azurocidin, the enrichment of this pathway suggests that arrhythmia-associated proteins are linked to mechanisms capable of promoting oxidative stress, extracellular matrix degradation, endothelial dysfunction, vascular leakage, and maladaptive inflammatory signaling. In cardiac tissue, these processes are especially relevant because excessive neutrophil granule release can intensify myocardial injury, alter structural remodeling, and contribute to the electrophysiological instability that underlies arrhythmia pathogenesis. The presence of 48 enriched proteins therefore provides numerical support for a biologically meaningful connection between dysregulated innate immune activation and cardiac electrical disease.

To further contextualize this enrichment signal, the interaction structure of the 48 proteins is shown below. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 48 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link for interactive inspection of network connectivity and functional associations.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
With that overall pathway context in place, the following proteins may be of particular interest because they could connect neutrophil degranulation-related biology to distinct aspects of arrhythmia susceptibility and remodeling.

ITGAV is among the most compelling candidates for relevance to arrhythmia because it links extracellular matrix remodeling, mechanotransduction, inflammation, and profibrotic signaling. Atrial and ventricular arrhythmias commonly emerge in structurally remodeled myocardium, particularly when fibrosis disrupts electrical continuity and conduction velocity. The reported role of ITGAV in adhesion to matrix ligands, angiogenesis, wound healing, and especially activation of latent transforming growth factor beta one is highly pertinent, because transforming growth factor beta signaling is a central driver of cardiac fibrosis and adverse remodeling. Through these mechanisms, ITGAV could contribute to the formation of an arrhythmogenic substrate characterized by conduction heterogeneity, fibroblast activation, and altered cell-matrix coupling. Its interactions with inflammatory and growth factor pathways further support a plausible role in post-injury remodeling and scar-associated arrhythmogenesis.[PubMed:10025398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) [PubMed:9827803](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9827803) [PubMed:25127859](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) [PubMed:11323698](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11323698) [PubMed:24935931](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24935931) 

In a related but somewhat more proteolytic dimension of remodeling, PRTN3 may also warrant attention. PRTN3 is notable in the context of arrhythmia because inflammatory and proteolytic remodeling are increasingly recognized as major contributors to atrial and ventricular electrical instability. By degrading elastin, fibronectin, laminin, vitronectin, and collagens, PRTN3 has the capacity to reshape the extracellular environment that supports myocardial architecture and impulse propagation. Its involvement in neutrophil transendothelial migration and inflammatory activation suggests a potential contribution to sterile inflammation after ischemia, myocarditis, or systemic inflammatory states, all of which can precipitate arrhythmias. Matrix degradation and inflammatory cell recruitment can favor fibrosis, gap-junction disorganization, and conduction slowing, thereby creating a substrate for reentry. Thus, although not a canonical ion-channel gene, PRTN3 stands out as a plausible mediator of inflammation-driven arrhythmogenic remodeling.[PubMed:2033050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2033050) [PubMed:28240246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28240246) [PubMed:3198760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3198760) [PubMed:23202369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23202369) [PubMed:22266279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22266279) [PubMed:36302784](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36302784) 

Extending from sterile inflammatory remodeling to infection-related injury, BST2 may represent another plausible connection. BST2 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because viral infection and dysregulated innate immunity are important causes of myocarditis and subsequent electrical instability. Its broad antiviral activity against multiple enveloped viruses, together with its ability to regulate interferon responses and nuclear factor kappa B signaling, suggests that BST2 could influence the balance between viral control and inflammatory injury in cardiac tissue. This is particularly important because viral myocarditis can evolve into atrial or ventricular arrhythmias through myocyte injury, edema, fibrosis, and altered conduction. The additional observation that BST2 can inhibit matrix metalloproteinase fourteen-dependent proteolytic activity also raises the possibility that it may influence matrix turnover and cell migration, both of which are relevant to structural remodeling. Therefore, BST2 stands out as an immune-modulatory protein with plausible mechanistic links to arrhythmia in infection-associated or inflammatory cardiac disease.[PubMed:18200009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [PubMed:18342597](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [PubMed:19036818](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [PubMed:19879838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [PubMed:20019814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [PubMed:20399176](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [PubMed:20419159](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [PubMed:20940320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [PubMed:21529378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [PubMed:22520941](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [PubMed:19179289](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19179289) [PubMed:20686043](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20686043) [PubMed:20943977](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20943977) [PubMed:21621240](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21621240) [PubMed:26378163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26378163) [PubMed:31199522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31199522) [PubMed:22065321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [PubMed:19564354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [PubMed:26172439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [PubMed:23028328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328) 

From the perspective of immune restraint rather than immune amplification, LAIR1 may also be relevant. LAIR1 is relevant to arrhythmia primarily through immune regulation. Cardiac arrhythmias, especially atrial fibrillation, are strongly associated with inflammatory signaling, immune-cell infiltration, and cytokine-mediated structural remodeling. LAIR1 functions as a broad inhibitory receptor that dampens immune activation, reduces proinflammatory cytokine production, and induces transforming growth factor beta in some contexts. This dual role suggests that LAIR1 may influence whether inflammation resolves or progresses toward fibrosis. In myocarditis, autoimmune injury, or chronic inflammatory remodeling, altered LAIR1 activity could affect the intensity of immune-mediated myocyte damage and subsequent fibrotic substrate formation. Its inhibition of nuclear factor kappa B signaling is particularly noteworthy, as this pathway is implicated in adverse remodeling and arrhythmia susceptibility.

Alongside immune regulation, vascular adaptation after injury may also be relevant to arrhythmogenic remodeling. CD93 may be meaningfully connected to arrhythmia through its role in vascular integrity and angiogenesis. Microvascular dysfunction, impaired tissue perfusion, and abnormal vascular remodeling can contribute to ischemic injury, atrial remodeling, and ventricular scar formation, each of which may predispose to arrhythmia. Because CD93 supports endothelial proliferation, migration, and vessel stability, it may influence how the myocardium responds to injury and whether repair is adaptive or maladaptive. In ischemic heart disease or heart failure, disturbed angiogenic signaling can exacerbate hypoxia and fibrosis, thereby promoting conduction heterogeneity. Although indirect, CD93 stands out as a vascular remodeling factor with plausible relevance to arrhythmogenic substrate development.[PubMed:28435016](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28435016) [PubMed:28671670](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28671670) [PubMed:28912033](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28912033) 

Another potentially related inflammatory axis involves complement activation. CFD is of interest because complement activation is increasingly implicated in cardiac inflammation, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and remodeling, all of which can facilitate arrhythmia. By driving activation of the alternative complement pathway, CFD may contribute to inflammatory tissue injury within the myocardium or vasculature. Complement-mediated inflammation can promote myocyte dysfunction, endothelial activation, fibroblast stimulation, and scar formation, thereby creating a substrate for abnormal impulse initiation and propagation. Thus, CFD is not directly electrophysiological, but it may participate in inflammatory mechanisms that are highly relevant to arrhythmia pathogenesis, especially in ischemic or immune-mediated settings.

Closely related to CFD, CFP may reinforce this same inflammatory framework. CFP complements the potential arrhythmia relevance of CFD by amplifying alternative pathway complement activity. Persistent or excessive complement activation may aggravate myocardial inflammation and tissue damage, particularly after ischemic injury or during systemic inflammatory states. Such processes can accelerate fibrosis, alter cell-cell coupling, and impair electrical conduction. Because CFP stabilizes the key convertase complexes of complement, it may enhance inflammatory cascades that indirectly favor arrhythmogenesis. This makes CFP a noteworthy candidate for involvement in inflammation-associated arrhythmic disease, even though its role is likely upstream and modulatory rather than directly causal at the level of ion handling.[PubMed:28264884](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28264884) 

Beyond complement biology, nucleic-acid sensing and mitochondrial homeostasis may provide another route toward electrical instability. RNASET2 is potentially important for arrhythmia because it sits at the intersection of innate immune sensing and mitochondrial ribonucleic acid homeostasis. Activation of toll-like receptor seven and toll-like receptor eight-dependent inflammatory pathways can contribute to myocarditis, systemic inflammation, and adverse cardiac remodeling, all recognized triggers of arrhythmia. In addition, mitochondrial dysfunction has major consequences for cardiomyocyte energetics, redox balance, and electrophysiological stability. A protein that regulates both immune activation by ribonucleic acid ligands and mitochondrial ribonucleic acid turnover may therefore influence susceptibility to inflammatory or metabolic forms of arrhythmogenesis. This makes RNASET2 an intriguing candidate, particularly in settings where viral infection or sterile nucleic-acid sensing contributes to cardiac electrical instability.[PubMed:31778653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31778653) [PubMed:38697119](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38697119) [PubMed:28730546](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28730546) [PubMed:30184494](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184494) [PubMed:30385512](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30385512) 

Metabolic and lysosomal pathways may also be relevant in a more indirect manner. NPC2 may be relevant to arrhythmia because cholesterol handling and lysosomal lipid trafficking influence membrane composition, receptor organization, and cellular stress responses. In the heart, altered lipid homeostasis can affect ion channel localization, membrane excitability, and cardiomyocyte viability. Lysosomal dysfunction and sterol accumulation are also associated with inflammatory activation and cellular injury, both of which can promote arrhythmogenic remodeling. While the connection is less direct than for fibrosis or inflammation genes, NPC2 stands out because metabolic and lysosomal disturbances are increasingly recognized contributors to cardiomyopathy-associated arrhythmias.[PubMed:12591949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12591949) [PubMed:17018531](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17018531) [PubMed:21315718](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21315718) [PubMed:26296895](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26296895) 

In contrast to these predominantly structural and inflammatory candidates, ADA2 may have a more direct relationship to electrophysiological control. ADA2 is directly relevant to arrhythmia because adrenergic signaling is a central regulator of cardiac automaticity, conduction, and triggered activity. Although alpha two adrenergic signaling is generally inhibitory through suppression of adenylate cyclase, changes in sympathetic-parasympathetic balance are fundamental in both atrial and ventricular arrhythmogenesis. Proteins that modulate catecholamine responses can influence heart rate, refractoriness, calcium handling, and susceptibility to stress-induced arrhythmias. Therefore, ADA2 stands out as one of the few proteins in the list with an explicit connection to neurohumoral signaling that could directly alter electrophysiological behavior.

At the systemic level, cardiometabolic inflammation may provide an additional explanatory layer. RETN is noteworthy because it connects metabolic dysfunction with inflammation, two major risk domains for arrhythmia, particularly atrial fibrillation. Obesity, insulin resistance, and diabetes are strongly associated with atrial structural remodeling, oxidative stress, autonomic imbalance, and low-grade inflammation. RETN may contribute to this pathophysiological milieu by promoting insulin resistance and myeloid-cell chemotaxis, thereby fostering both metabolic and inflammatory stress. These processes can accelerate atrial fibrosis and electrical remodeling, increasing arrhythmia susceptibility. Thus, RETN is a plausible systemic mediator linking cardiometabolic disease to arrhythmic risk.[PubMed:15064728](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15064728) 

Related to this intersection of inflammation and signaling, S100P may also merit consideration. S100P is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because calcium signaling abnormalities are fundamental drivers of triggered activity, conduction instability, and excitation-contraction dysfunction. As a calcium-binding signaling protein, S100P may influence intracellular calcium-dependent pathways, and its ability to signal through receptor for advanced glycation end products suggests an additional inflammatory axis. Receptor for advanced glycation end products-associated signaling has been implicated in oxidative stress, fibrosis, and diabetic cardiovascular remodeling, all of which can predispose to arrhythmia. Although the evidence here is indirect, the combination of calcium-sensing and inflammatory signaling makes S100P a biologically plausible contributor to arrhythmogenic remodeling.

Finally, NFASC may be considered within a more speculative neurocardiac framework. NFASC has a more speculative but still potentially meaningful connection to arrhythmia through autonomic regulation. Cardiac rhythm is strongly influenced by the autonomic nervous system, and proteins involved in neuronal adhesion, axonal organization, and synaptic development may affect neural circuitry that modulates cardiac excitability. Although NFASC is primarily characterized in the nervous system rather than myocardium, altered autonomic innervation is an established contributor to both atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. Therefore, NFASC may be relevant indirectly through neurocardiac mechanisms rather than direct myocardial electrophysiology.
